Bloc set is data-driven from app/public/data/bvar/gvar/weights_24bloc.json (blocs field, US first; the 24 in the filename is historical — the app fetches this file from the data pack at runtime and checks its hash; a compiled copy is only the module-load default). It holds the 35 shipped blocs, the same list as weights_full_38.json — copy weights_full_38.json over weights_24bloc.json when the topology changes (§3.0). The US is the first entry and has a weights.US row, which is what makes it endogenous.

docs.title: 1. Re-estimate the GVAR macro blocs (GVAR-EM loop)
1.1 What the loop does
docs.text:
pipeline/export_bvar_gvar24_loop.m is the canonical GVAR-EM (Expectation–Maximization) estimator:

  1. For each non-US bloc, build its 3 RoW "star" vars (ROWDEM/ROWINF/ROWFIN) = trade-weighted averages of partners' real-GDP growth / inflation / short rate, renormalised over the partners present each quarter (unbalanced panel). COVID + no-partner quarters start NaN.
  2. Estimate each bloc by cgl_bvarV5([domestic | 3 stars]) — the COVID-as-missing Gibbs sampler; the DK (Durbin–Koopman) smoother fills the missing star + COVID quarters → a completed matrix per bloc.
  3. Loop (Jacobi): recompute every bloc's stars from partners' completed data, re-estimate all blocs in parallel (parfor), until the foreign components converge (max |Δstar| < TOL).

Key facts encoded in the script (do not change without re-validating):

  • US_ENDOGENOUS=1 (env). With a weights.US row present, the US is folded into the convergence loop and re-estimated with its own 3 RoW stars (n=40 today: domestic + fiscal + globals + 3 ROW*_US). It drives RoW and receives RoW→US feedback. A no-stars bootstrap still runs first only to seed partners' iter-1 stars (it is discarded, not exported).
  • COVID window is the argmin of ΔGDP restricted to 2019Q4–2021Q1 (a global argmin misfires, e.g. KR's 2008Q4 GFC drop), then ± quarters around it are NaN'd → DK-imputed.
  • MAXIT=12, TOL=0.03 (MC noise floor ≈0.13 — unless GVAR_FIXHYPER=1, production since Oct 2026, which holds (λ, μ) at the mode with aligned random numbers during the sweeps so the loop really converges; the 2026 run used MAXIT=30 and converged at sweep 6, then ran one full-MH pass). MAXIT=1 ⇒ single-country (separated): one-shot historical stars, no coupling iteration.
  • Scale traps (already correct in-script, listed so you don't "fix" them): stars are 4·Δ(100·log) not 400·; the completed panel is mean(Xcond,3); CN GDP is real (since the 2026-06 CN-only re-estimate; NOMINAL_GDP_BLOCS empty) → read directly, not deflated by subtraction; leading star NaN is back-filled (not under GVAR_NOFILL=1, production since Oct 2026: every gap stays missing and is drawn by the sampler); the _US column is dropped (no-op on _glob inputs); the short rate is optional (CH/NO have none → excluded from partners' ROWFIN); AR hyperinflation excluded from partners' INF/FIN (kept in DEM).

docs.title: 1.2 Run it
docs.text:
From the repo root (MATLAB with the Parallel Computing Toolbox; the loop uses parfor):

# Full 35-bloc endogenous-US run — the October 2026 production settings (about 1 h 40 min).
# Exact script: docs/reest-2026/runs/run_gvar35b.sh
BVAR_DIFF_GP=1 US_ENDOGENOUS=1 NDRAWS=1000 MAXIT=30 BVAR_SEED=1 GVAR_FIXHYPER=1 GVAR_NOFILL=1 \
  GVAR_WEIGHTS_FILE="$PWD/app/public/data/bvar/gvar/weights_full_38.json" \
  GVAR_DUMMY_BLOCS="CL CN CO CR EA ID IL IN IS JP KR MX NO TR UK ZA HK PE" \
  BVAR_RAWDATA_DIR="$PWD/pipeline/country_rawdata" GVAR_OUTDIR=<run>/gvar35 GVAR_WORKSPACE=<run>/gvar35_ws.mat \
  matlab -batch "run('pipeline/export_bvar_gvar24_loop.m')"

weights_full_38.json holds the 35 shipped blocs (the name is historical; Israel is still in the dummy list but no longer estimated). GVAR_DUMMY_BLOCS must be passed explicitly to add HK+PE to the seasonal-dummy set — the script's own default is the 16-bloc set (§1.3), so without the override the two new NSA-seasonal blocs would estimate without their quarterly dummies. Time-varying weights (weights_timevarying.json) are picked up automatically for the estimation stars when present (§1.3(c)) — no env flag needed.

Useful env overrides (for fast subset validation before committing the multi-hour full run):

# Fast smoke: 3 blocs, few draws, 1 iteration (single-country, no coupling)
BVAR_GVAR_BLOCS="US EA JP" NDRAWS=200 MAXIT=1 US_ENDOGENOUS=1 \
  matlab -batch "run('pipeline/export_bvar_gvar24_loop.m')"
Env Default Meaning US_ENDOGENOUS unset (anchor) 1 ⇒ US is a coupled bloc (requires weights.US). Set it for production. BVAR_GVAR_BLOCS all blocs in weights file space-separated subset, US first NDRAWS 1000 (burn = 500) MCMC draws per bloc MAXIT 12 max convergence sweeps (1 = separated); 2026 run: 30 BVAR_DIFF_GP unset 1 ⇒ real GDP and prices in differences (growth rates) — the shipped model GVAR_NOFILL unset 1 ⇒ no fills: every gap is missing data drawn by the sampler; exports estimation_mask.json (needs BVAR_DIFF_GP=1). Production since Oct 2026 GVAR_FIXHYPER unset 1 ⇒ smooth EM sweeps ((λ, μ) at the mode, aligned random numbers) + a final full-MH pass. Production since Oct 2026 BVAR_SEED unset random seed (2026: 1) BVAR_RAWDATA_DIR pipeline/country_rawdata read the panels from another folder (strict: no fallback) GVAR_OUTDIR / GVAR_WORKSPACE /tmp/gvar24_export / /tmp/gvar24_workspace.mat where exports and the workspace go TOL 0.03 convergence tol on max |Δstar| GVAR_WEIGHTS_FILE weights_full.json else weights_24bloc.json which weights/bloc list to use; production passes weights_full_38.json (35 blocs) GVAR_DUMMY_BLOCS the 16-bloc default set (§1.3) space-separated override of the seasonal-dummy blocs; production passes 18 codes (16 + HK + PE) GVAR_TV_WEIGHTS on if the artifact exists 0 ⇒ static weights everywhere (byte-identical legacy). Reads weights_timevarying.json (now promoted to app/public/data/bvar/gvar/; §1.3) GVAR_NSA_FORECAST unset ⇒ SA forward forecast for seasonal (nsr=3) blocs the shipped forward forecast is seasonally adjusted (annual-mean deterministic term); 1 ⇒ keep the quarter-specific NSA forecast (§1.3(d)) GVAR_POLISH_EXACT off 1 ⇒ run the optional final exact-DA polish sweep. Off for the shipped coupled models — the polish lifts ρ(M)>1 (§1.3 / two-stage)

See §1.3 for the seasonal-v2 knobs (GVAR_DUMMY_BLOCS, GVAR_TV_WEIGHTS, GVAR_NSA_FORECAST, GVAR_POLISH_EXACT, CGL_FIXED_COMPANION) and the two-stage E-step rationale.

Outputs. Each bloc's full deployed JSON contract to GVAR_OUTDIR (default /tmp/gvar24_export/<CC>/) (spec, companion_mean, companion_draws, historical, historical_levels, baseline, baseline_levels, transformations, and under GVAR_NOFILL=1 estimation_mask.json — the cells the sampler drew, which the app shows as model estimates). The full estimation state is also saved to /tmp/gvar24_workspace.mat before export, so an export-only bug is a cheap re-export, not a re-estimation.

Watch the console. Each iteration prints max star change vs tol; convergence prints CONVERGED. Each export prints n, draws, and the 1-quarter GDP growth (GDP1q) — confirm it is a sane number, not NaN or a collapsed flat line.

If a bloc returns a singular / NaN SIGMA, the data is the cause (a leading NaN in a discontinued series, or near-collinear national-accounts identities). Fix the raw DataRaw_<CC>_glob.json, not the estimator. With COVID imputed the empirical-Bayes lambda optimum is well-behaved (~0.24–0.56); a fixed lamfix is not needed (and pinning one with noc/sur both fixed makes lambda degenerate to NaN).

docs.title: 1.3 Seasonal-v2 estimation (dummies · two-stage E-step · time-varying weights)
docs.text:
Three estimation features (2026-07-17, all env-gated, all byte-identical no-ops when off) travel with the loop. They matter for the NSA-seasonal and coupon-lumpy blocs.

(a) Quarterly seasonal dummies — GVAR_DUMMY_BLOCS. Blocs with a genuinely NSA-seasonal series (calendar-R²≥0.40 and display-amplitude ≥2 on the panel scan — NSA HICP/CPI, unemployment, house prices, some SFA/GOV series) plus every even-interest bloc (§2.3) get quarterly dummies D=[q==2, q==3, q==4] (Q1 the base) in each equation, so the seasonal cycle is a bounded deterministic cycle rather than a spurious near-Nyquist explosive root. The default coupled set (verified pipeline/export_bvar_gvar24_loop.m:49–53) is:

CL CN CO CR EA ID IL IN IS JP KR MX NO TR UK ZA        # 16 coupled blocs (GVAR_DUMMY_BLOCS default)

The 38-bloc run passes 18. The two new NSA-seasonal FSAP blocs — HK and PE — are not in the in-script default, so the production 38-bloc command explicitly sets GVAR_DUMMY_BLOCS="… HK PE" (§1.2). SG/RO/PH do not carry the dummies (they did not clear the NSA-seasonal panel scan). Verify the console print GVAR-EM: seasonal-dummy blocs: … lists all 18.

plus the six euro members ES IT GR PT SI BE handled by the standalone estimator (pipeline/export_bvar_euro_redesign.m:44–49, env EURO_DUMMY_MEMBERS). Mechanism (verified BVAR/MFBVAR/Support/BVAR.m:4–6,63,74): the design row is x=[1, D, y_{t-1},…,y_{t-p}], so betahat has k = 1 + nsr + n·lags rows laid out [constant; γQ2; γQ3; γQ4; B_1;…;B_p] with nsr=3 ("seasonalRows"); the dummy coefficients carry the diffuse intercept prior (Vc=1e6) and are zeroed in the sum-of-coefficients dummy observations. cgl_bvarV5.m receives the per-row quarter-of-year via the 'qoy' vararg (the DK simulation-smoother artificial path carries the seasonal term, and the forecast simulation continues the q-of-year cycle). exportbloc ships seasonalRows in spec.json + companion_mean.json (and qoyNext for seasonal blocs); legacy nsr=0 blocs are bit-for-bit unchanged.

Phase rule (do not hand-carry qoyNext). The app always recomputes qoyNext from its own date grid via dates.qoyNextOf(country) (= the quarter after lastHistOf, wrapped 1..4; app/src/lib/dates.ts:88–89), never the shipped estimation-grid qoyNext (which sits one quarter behind after the production shift; app/src/lib/compute/gvarSolve.ts:417–422). The shipped qoyNext is only for the node pipeline scripts (qoyNextOverride).

(b) Two-stage E-step — GVAR_POLISH_EXACT (default OFF for the coupled system) + CGL_FIXED_COMPANION. The outer Jacobi/EM loop runs the DK imputation with a fixed-companion E-step (cgl_bvarV5 'fixedcomp',1) so consecutive sweeps share random numbers (common random numbers) and the star fixed point contracts to TOL (export_bvar_gvar24_loop.m:159–195). The shipped coupled models use the fixed-companion posterior from that converged loop. A textbook exact data-augmentation E-step (companion rebuilt from the current draw every Gibbs sweep — the open-issue-#4 fix, env CGL_FIXED_COMPANION=0 / 'fixedcomp',0) is available as an optional final polish sweep at the frozen converged stars (:197–217, GVAR_POLISH_EXACT=1) but is OFF by default: exact DA (i) breaks the CRN contraction if used inside the loop (a ~0.6–1.8pp star-churn floor that never meets TOL) and (ii) marginally raises companion persistence, which lifts the coupled operator's ρ(M) above 1 (measured 1.0067 with the polish vs <1 without) → non-contractive pinned-scenario spillovers. So keep it off for the coupled ship; enable GVAR_POLISH_EXACT=1 only for a standalone exact-DA reference posterior. Single-bloc estimators (euro members) run exact DA directly and are unaffected.

(c) Time-varying trade weights — GVAR_TV_WEIGHTS + weights_timevarying.json (now promoted for estimation). When app/public/data/bvar/gvar/weights_timevarying.json exists and GVAR_TV_WEIGHTS≠0, buildstars applies each quarter's calendar-year weight row (clamped to the file's span; a partner absent from a year's row gets weight 0, absorbed by the existing per-component renormalization — export_bvar_gvar24_loop.m:55–72,269–318). Absent artifact or GVAR_TV_WEIGHTS=0 ⇒ the static row everywhere (byte-identical legacy).

  • Source it: pipeline/fsap_expansion_staging/weights/build_weights_timevarying.py pulls IMF IMTS via api.imf.org SDMX 2.1 (dataset IMTS, indicators XG_FOB_USD+MG_CIF_USD, key COUNTRY.INDICATOR.COUNTERPART.A), annual bilateral X+M 1995–2024 over 39 blocs (the 38 coupled + AE), per-year row-normalized (zero diagonal, <0.05% shares dropped) → weights_timevarying.json (+ weights_latest.json = 2024, + weights_validation.json).
  • Promote it: copy the staged weights_timevarying.json into app/public/data/bvar/gvar/ — done on the seasonal-v2 branch (the artifact is now present there), so the loop reads it and GVAR_TV_WEIGHTS is active by default during estimation. weights_full_38.json (the static coupling file) is the 2021–23 average of this same TV panel over the 38-bloc set.

Note the solve-time coupling still uses the static file (weights_24bloc.json) — the estimation stars are time-varying, but the browser (I−M)⁻¹ operator is built from the static/current-year weights; swapping the coupling to the latest year would be a separate, user-approved step. Honest empirical shape (validation artifact): the US→China trade share rises to a mid-2010s peak (~0.17) then FALLS after the 2018 trade war (~0.12 by 2024), while US→euro-area does not decline — it rises (~0.178 by 2024). Document the reversal; do not claim a monotone CN-up / EA-down trend.

(d) Seasonally-adjusted forward forecast — GVAR_NSA_FORECAST (2026-07-18). The quarterly dummies of §1.3(a) stay in estimation and the DK imputation (quarter-specific), but the shipped forward forecast is seasonally adjusted: for a seasonal (nsr=3) bloc the deterministic term uses the annual-mean dummy row [¼,¼,¼] at every step, so the baseline is c̄ = c + (γ_{Q2}+γ_{Q3}+γ_{Q4})/4 (a smooth SA path that matches cgl_bvarV5's SA Dforecast bands + the app — verified export_bvar_gvar24_loop.m:339–350, cgl_bvarV5.m:255–266). Setting GVAR_NSA_FORECAST=1 switches the forward forecast back to the quarter-specific (NSA) path (drow=[q==2,q==3,q==4]). Leave it unset for the shipped models (SA baseline). Legacy nsr=0 blocs are unaffected either way.

docs.title: 1.4 DVAX difference-form foreign-demand prior (shipped in 3.3.0, rolled back in 3.4.0 — NOT in the current model)
docs.text:
The October 2026 re-estimation does not use DVAX (no BVAR_FMEAN_MAP / BVAR_KAPPA_ROW / BVAR_NOC_EXEMPT_STARS in docs/reest-2026/runs/run_gvar35b.sh). Kept for reference.

The 3.3.0 model re-centred the foreign-demand star only (ROWDEM → GDP; inflation and the foreign-rate star keep the standard prior) onto each bloc's value-added export share μ_i = EXGR_DVA/VALU (OECD–WTO TiVA, per-country in pipeline/mu_dvax.json). Units matter: ROWDEM is an annualized growth rate and domestic GDP carries the RW own-lag prior (its equation is a quarterly first difference), so the prior mean is +μ_i/4 on lag-1 and −μ_i/4 on lag-2 — a difference (coefficients sum to zero → no permanent drift, only transitory co-movement). Reduced form has no lag-0, so "contemporaneous"→lag-1, "first lag"→lag-2. The mechanism is a lag-aware fmean set at both prior-mean sites (BVAR_coint.m draws + cgl_bvarV5_coint.m MH target), with κ=0.15 on ROWDEM and ROWDEM noc-exempt.

# Env flags on top of the §1.2 run (level mode: BVAR_GROWTH_SPACE UNSET):
US_ENDOGENOUS=1 \
BVAR_FMEAN_MAP=1 \                 # per-country μ from pipeline/mu_dvax.json (via the muMap arg — parfor-safe)
BVAR_KAPPA_ROW=0.15 \             # tight κ on ROWDEM only
BVAR_NOC_EXEMPT_STARS=1 \        # ROWDEM noc-exempt
NDRAWS=1000 MAXIT=12 \
GVAR_WEIGHTS_FILE=<abs>/app/public/data/bvar/gvar/weights_full_38.json \
GVAR_OUTDIR=/tmp/gvar24_dvax \
matlab -batch "run('pipeline/export_bvar_gvar24_loop.m')"

Coefficient gate (before trusting the run): per bloc, exported betahat, GDP equation — ROWDEM lag-1 ≈ +μ_i/4, lag-2 ≈ −μ_i/4 (US ±0.024), lag-3 ≈ 0; ROWINF/ROWFIN unchanged. The Minnesota lag decay (α=2) makes the lag-2 prior ~4× tighter than lag-1, so lag-1 is the more data-pulled of the two — expected, not a defect. Then the usual gates: dense-eig ρ(M) ≤ 0.985 (the stored JS power-iteration under-reads ~0.003 — always dense-eig; §4.1), and the US-spread global solve in the paper ballpark. Euro members are re-estimated separately (CC=<code> matlab -batch "run('pipeline/export_bvar_euro_redesign.m')" per member, staging → §3 port). Full config: docs/dvax-rowdem-level-config.md.

Honest limit. The prior shapes the pass-through to domestic GDP, not ROWDEM's own dynamics — the star can still drift under its RW prior, but because the net pass-through b¹+b²≈0, domestic GDP inherits almost none of it (the level system stays anchored). A handful of EM blocs (BR/CN/JP) keep a marginally-explosive own companion; the world read-out is delta-aggregated so it is immune (§3.3 / the manual's Known-issues note).

docs.title: 2. Rebuild the fiscal block (4-variable, exact-residual SFA)
docs.text:
Since October 2026 the fiscal block of all 41 fiscal economies is built inside the panel build from each source registry's fiscal section (pipeline/sources/registry/README.md: revenue, total expenditure, interest, gross debt and nominal GDP from their publishers; a genuine GDP deflator column; even-coupon economies use trailing 4-quarter interest ÷ debt). The per-country builders below are the older path; the identities (SFA as the exact residual of the app's debt recursion) are unchanged.

The fiscal block carries 4 estimated BVAR variables (originally for US, EA, JP, UK, CA, CN):

ID Meaning Units FREV_GDP revenue / GDP × 100 % of GDP (annual) FPEXP_GDP primary expenditure / GDP × 100 % of GDP (annual) EFFI effective interest rate = net interest / lagged gross debt × 100, annualised % p.a. SFA stock-flow adjustment % of GDP (annual)

SFA is the exact residual of the app's debt recursion. The build script rearranges the exact recursion in app/src/lib/compute/fiscalAccounting.ts (computeFiscalBlock, ~line 169) onto the observed gross-debt/GDP path so that the BVAR's SFA column closes the recursion to machine precision (it captures the federal-flows-vs-gross-debt perimeter seam / intragovernmental holdings — the deficit–debt discrepancy):

d_t = d_{t-1}·(1 + EFFI/400)/(1 + gNomQ/100) − pb/4 + sfa/4        (% of GDP)
pb     = FREV_GDP − FPEXP_GDP
gNomQ  = 100·log(realGDP_t/realGDP_{t-1}) + 100·log(deflator_t/deflator_{t-1})   (% per quarter)
⇒ SFA_t = 4·(d_obs_t − d_{t-1} − snowball_t + pb_t/4)

The crucial subtlety: gNomQ is read off the same glob columns the app reads (idx.gdp/idx.deflator, stored as 100·log), as a log growth — not a simple nominal SAAR (seasonally-adjusted annualised rate) growth. Building it the app's way is what drives the closure error to < 1e-6 (an interpolated COVID value can never equal the residual, so COVID quarters are set NaN for the Gibbs to impute).

fiscal_meta/<CC>.json carries idx = {gdp, deflator, revenue, primaryExp, effRate, sfa} (note: there is no debtService — DSVC was reverted to EFFI), d0, and sfaDefault. The debt/GDP projection now carries the forecast SFA forward (idx.sfa set ⇒ the recursion reads the estimated SFA level path with its own dynamics + bands, instead of defaulting SFA to 0).

docs.title: 2.1 Run the builds
docs.text:
One script per fiscal economy. They are data-build only (no estimation, no network): each edits only the SFA column of DataRaw_<CC>_glob.json in place (everything else byte-identical), sets the COVID window to NaN, runs the closure check, and writes sfaDefault (the non-COVID, ex-t0 SFA mean) into fiscal_meta/<CC>.json.

cd "<repo root>/pipeline"
python3 build_fiscal_us_4var.py
python3 build_fiscal_ea_4var.py
python3 build_fiscal_jp_4var.py
python3 build_fiscal_uk_4var.py
python3 build_fiscal_ca_4var.py
python3 build_fiscal_cn_4var.py

The gate is automatic and hard: each script asserts the one-step closure |d_obs_t − recon_t| < 1e-6 for every non-COVID quarter t≥1 and aborts on failure. It prints backcastMaxErrPP (must be ~1e-13), the SFA range, and the chosen sfaDefault.

Current sfaDefault (≈ non-COVID SFA mean, % of GDP) — sanity benchmarks after a rebuild:

US EA JP UK CA CN sfaDefault 1.75 0.33 2.23 3.15 3.19 4.02

Order: rebuild the fiscal SFA before re-estimating the GVAR if the fiscal data changed — the SFA column lives in the same DataRaw_<CC>_glob.json the GVAR-EM loop reads. If only the macro data changed, the fiscal SFA still must be rebuilt so the residual stays exact against the new gdp/deflator levels.

docs.title: 2.2 (Optional) refresh the human-checkable walkthrough
docs.text:
A reviewer-facing Excel walkthrough of the US/UK fiscal accounting lives at docs/fiscal_accounting_walkthrough_US_UK.xlsx (the user's source is docs/Fiscal_Accounting_US_UK_NSA.xlsx). Regenerate it after a fiscal rebuild:

python3 pipeline/build_fiscal_walkthrough_xlsx.py

docs.title: 2.3 Even-coupon EFFI rebuild (coupon-lumpy RoW fiscal blocs)
docs.text:
The wider RoW fiscal blocs are built by pipeline/build_fiscal22_columns.py (which appends the same four FREV_GDP/FPEXP_GDP/EFFI/SFA columns to a bloc's _glob.json). Eight of them pay interest on an annual/semiannual coupon calendar, which made the single-quarter EFFI a near-Nyquist sawtooth (the diagnosed root cause of the EFFI/SFA jaggedness). For these blocs the builder distributes the coupon evenly before estimation (verified pipeline/build_fiscal22_columns.py:58–100,178–181):

EVEN_INTEREST = {CL, CO, CR, ID, IL, MX, TR, ZA}     # coupon-lumpy blocs (calendar-R²>0.5 & CV>0.25)

even_distribute_years() replaces the 4 quarterly interest payments within each complete calendar year by their mean (annual total preserved exactly; a trailing partial year uses the trailing-4Q mean), so EFFI = 400·evened_interest_t / debt_{t-1} becomes the accrual borrowing cost. Primary expenditure keeps the raw interest (te − intr = true non-interest spending), and the exact debt-identity residual SFA absorbs the genuine cash-vs-accrual timing — which is why these eight blocs also carry seasonal dummies (§1.3). The debt identity still closes to ~1e-14, and the sawtooth companion root moves off −1 (e.g. ZA −0.973→−0.634). Full mechanism + the before/after numbers: fiscal-block-methodology.md. Rebuild is --force (the columns already exist in the panel):

cd "<repo root>/pipeline"
python3 build_fiscal22_columns.py --force          # re-appends the 4 fiscal cols; even-coupon EFFI for EVEN_INTEREST

Run this before the GVAR-EM loop if the RoW fiscal data changed (the columns live in the same DataRaw_<CC>_glob.json the loop reads), and re-estimate with <CC> ∈ EVEN_INTEREST in GVAR_DUMMY_BLOCS (they are in the default set, §1.3).

docs.title: 3. Port the exports into the app
docs.text:
Since October 2026: the 35 GVAR blocs are copied raw (full precision, incl. estimation_mask.json) and only the 17 euro members go through port_gvar_exports.py (6 significant figures); the fiscal metas come from the panel build; both fix_fiscal_meta_indices.mjs and fix_external_meta_indices.mjs run after the port. Exact commands: docs/reest-2026/runs/port_to_app.sh. The rest of §3 is the older 6-sig-fig path, kept for reference.

The post-run chain (FACT sequence): inspect/quality-gate the exports → port → swap the runtime weights (§3.0) → refresh + re-index fiscal_meta (§3.1) → regen coupling (§3.2) → rebuild the coverage manifest (§3.3) → 2026Q1 rebase (§3.4) → green gate (§4).

# Ports EVERY bloc present in the export dir, compacting to 6 significant figures + compact JSON.
python3 pipeline/port_gvar_exports.py

# Restrict to specific blocs, or dry-run to report sizes:
GVAR_PORT_BLOCS="US EA JP" python3 pipeline/port_gvar_exports.py
python3 pipeline/port_gvar_exports.py --dry-run

This copies /tmp/gvar24_export/<CC>/*.json → app/public/data/bvar/<CC>/*.json at the deployed 6-significant-figure precision.

docs.title: 3.0 Swap the runtime weights file (ONLY when the bloc set changed)
docs.text:
The app reads weights_24bloc.json (the filename is historical): it fetches it from the data pack at runtime and checks it against the manifest hash; the copy compiled into gvarSolve.ts is only the module-load default. When the topology changes, promote the new bloc list by copying the estimation source over it, so the runtime configureGVARTopology sees every bloc:

cp app/public/data/bvar/gvar/weights_full_38.json app/public/data/bvar/gvar/weights_24bloc.json

Both files share the load-bearing {blocs, weights} schema (US first, weights.US row present). Do this before the coupling regen (§3.2) — the coupling operator's dimension is derived from this bloc list. On a pure re-estimate of the existing set (no new bloc), skip this step.

Seasonal contract is per-bloc and carried through porting. seasonalRows (0 or 3) and, for seasonal blocs, qoyNext ship inside each bloc's spec.json/companion_mean.json (and the draws' beta_shape k = 1 + nsr + n·lags), so the porter just copies them — nothing extra to wire per bloc. Every downstream consumer reads seasonalRows and re-phases on the app grid: the loader/solver (gvarSolve.buildParams), and the post-run scripts app/scripts/refresh-quarter.mjs, nowcast_complete.mjs, precompute_gvar_coupling.mjs, member_extend.mjs, regen_gvar_bands.mjs are all seasonal-aware (they guard the k = 1 + nsr + n·lags layout and thread qoyNext from the app's own dates, per §1.3). A nsr=0 bloc flows through every one of them byte-identically to before.

docs.title: 3.1 Refresh the app fiscal_meta
docs.text:
The app reads fiscal_meta per country at app/public/data/bvar/<CC>/fiscal_meta.json. Copy the freshly built pipeline metas over:

# Oct 2026 (41 fiscal economies): GVAR blocs from the panel build, euro members from their staging folder
for cc in <fiscal GVAR blocs>; do cp "pipeline/country_rawdata/fiscal_meta_$cc.json" "app/public/data/bvar/$cc/fiscal_meta.json"; done
for cc in <euro members>;      do cp "pipeline/euro_redesign_staging/$cc/fiscal_meta.json" "app/public/data/bvar/$cc/fiscal_meta.json"; done
# (older six-bloc form: cp pipeline/fiscal_meta/<CC>.json app/public/data/bvar/<CC>/fiscal_meta.json)

RULE — re-index the fiscal meta after porting (MANDATORY on any variable-order change). Run node pipeline/fix_fiscal_meta_indices.mjs. fiscal_meta.json indexes the fiscal drivers by column POSITION; any change to a bloc's variable order/count (the GVAR-EM refit inserts variables ahead of the fiscal block in every spec except US) silently re-points those indices at the WRONG columns — the cause of an earlier EA/UK debt explosion (EA's effRate landed on the equity index ~col 537). port_gvar_exports.py now re-resolves the meta for the blocs it ports; raw-copied GVAR blocs need the script. fix_fiscal_meta_indices.mjs re-resolves the indices by variable id from the deployed spec.json and rewrites every fiscal meta, preserving d0/sfaDefault; it is idempotent (prints ok when nothing moved). Run it after every port that touches a fiscal bloc — a stale index can pass tsc/build and still ship a wrong debt path.

node pipeline/fix_fiscal_meta_indices.mjs    # re-resolves idx{gdp,deflator,revenue,primaryExp,effRate,sfa} by id
node pipeline/fix_external_meta_indices.mjs  # same for external_meta.json (idx from its stored idxIds)

The external re-index was added in October 2026, when inserting DEFL_<CC> re-pointed the exchange-rate index in 35 external_meta.json files. The test app/src/__tests__/data/meta-column-indices.test.ts guards both files.

docs.title: 3.2 Regenerate the GVAR coupling artifact (MANDATORY after any bloc data change)
docs.text:
The browser solves the cross-country fixed point x = (I−M)⁻¹ d from a pre-shipped coupling artifact. At this scale the in-browser inverse is many minutes — pre-shipping is mandatory, not an optimisation. With the endogenous US the artifact is the augmented (stars ++ US-global) operator. The dimension is #blocs·60 + 80: the shipped 35-bloc artifact (pack 2026Q2-reest-20261008b) is dim = 2180 (35·60 + 80), ρ(M) = 0.971875 (rhoSpectral in coupling_default.json.gz). (Earlier: 33 blocs, dim 2060, ρ 0.945494; September 2026, 35 blocs, ρ 0.957724.) Read the live dim/rhoSpectral off the artifact header after regen (§4.1); what is load-bearing is that ρ(M) < 1. Keyed to the data by modelSig.

From app/ (the script builds M in JS, then inverts (I−M) via MATLAB BLAS — the invert_coupling.py NumPy path is the no-MATLAB fallback). Use vite-node, not node (the script imports the TS compute modules):

cd app
npx vite-node scripts/precompute_gvar_coupling.mjs

It writes the gzipped app/public/data/bvar/gvar/coupling_default.json.gz directly (the plain .json is removed — at this bloc count it exceeds GitHub's 100 MB per-file limit; gzip ≈ 36 MB at 35 blocs). The data-pack manifest records the hash of the weights the coupling was built from, and the app ignores a coupling whose weights do not match the served ones. The loader decompresses it via the browser's native DecompressionStream. The artifact is keyed to the data by modelSig, so it MUST be regenerated whenever any deployed bloc changes — a stale artifact (modelSig mismatch) is rejected and the app falls back to the slow path.

docs.title: 3.3 Rebuild the coverage / provenance manifest
docs.text:
The app ships app/public/data/coverage_manifest.json describing each bloc's variable coverage and data provenance (it also reads nowcast_provenance.json). After the port (and any bloc-set change), rebuild it so the new blocs and their coverage are reflected:

cd app
node scripts/build_coverage_manifest.mjs      # → app/public/data/coverage_manifest.json

(Plain node here — this script does not import the TS compute modules.) The October 2026 chain ran it as npx vite-node scripts/build_coverage_manifest.mjs --panel-quarter 2026Q2 (the flag asserts the expected panel quarter). Commit the regenerated manifest alongside the ported bloc JSONs, and re-stamp the data pack (node scripts/pack-build.mjs --pack-id <new id>).

docs.title: 3.4 2026Q1 rebase (shift the display origin without re-estimating) — history
docs.text:
This is how the earlier 2025Q4 estimate was brought to the 2026Q1 origin. The October 2026 re-estimation fits every model to all data published through 2026Q2, so no shift follows it; its ragged edge is nowcast inside the chain (★ step 4). The next data shift (2026Q3) uses npm run data:shift (UPDATE_MANUAL.md §6).

The companion is estimated once on the 2025Q4 vintage and then shifted forward quarterly without re-estimating — this is the "estimate once, shift quarterly" method. After a fresh 2025Q4 re-estimation the display origin sits at 2025Q4 (each history ends at the estimation end — its own firstQuarter + rows says so); to promote to the 2026Q1 production origin:

  1. 2026Q1 becomes the last observation = genuine real-time releases where available + a cross-bloc G-BVAR nowcast for the missing ragged-edge cells (the coupled solve fills the 2026Q1 holes). 2026Q2 is then the first forecast.
  2. Run the two seasonal-aware shift scripts from app/ (vite-node, not node — they import the TS compute modules; the exact flags + orchestration order are in data-refresh-rollout.md): 
    cd app
npx vite-node scripts/refresh-quarter.mjs --bloc US --asof 2026Q1 --accept-revisions   # genuine observed row for the WIRED bloc(s)
npx vite-node scripts/nowcast_complete.mjs --to 2026Q1 --write --baselines             # one coupled solve fills every ragged edge
  3. 4.0: there is no date to set. The appended row is dated by the history's own calendar (firstQuarter + rows − 1). In practice run the whole chain instead of the two scripts: npm run data:model-update -- --then-shift (after the re-export), or npm run data:shift -- --asof 2026Q1 --commit.

These scripts guard the seasonal k = 1 + nsr + n·lags betahat layout and re-phase qoyNext on the app's own grid (§1.3 phase rule). Full quarterly-shift procedure (provenance, vintages archive, member-extend): data-refresh-rollout.md.

docs.title: 4. Verify (the green gate — do not skip)
4.1 Fast GVAR coupling / fixed-point gate
docs.text:
cd app
NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=8192 npx tsx scripts/verify_gvar24.mjs

Uses the shipped artifact (no live rebuild). Checks: (1) artifact modelSig matches the deployed blocs (else STALE — re-run §3.2); (2) the shipped inverse really is the inverse (max|(I−M)·invImM − I| small); (3) ρ(M) < 1 and matches the stored value; (4) Gauss-Seidel ≡ artifact-seeded closed form for representative shocks.

docs.title: 4.2 Type-check, tests, build
docs.text:
cd app
npx tsc --noEmit
npx vitest run          # ALL must pass — watch the canaries
BASE_PATH=/bvar-scenario npm run build

Canary / regression tests to watch (in app/src/__tests__/compute/):

  • Fiscal: fiscalAccounting.test.ts, fiscal-backcast.test.ts, fiscal-conditioning-integration.test.ts — the debt back-cast and the SFA-forward projection.
  • GVAR: gvar-us-endogenous.test.ts, gvar-coupling-artifact.test.ts (artifact ≡ live), gvar-closed-form-routing.test.ts, gvar-derived-topology.test.ts, gvar-direct-coupling-strip-equivalence.test.ts, gvar-convergence.test.ts, gvar-band-solve.test.ts.
  • Scale canary: scenario-scale-convention.test.ts — if n changed, its fixture may be pinned to the old layout; regenerate via pipeline/_verify/gt.m (resolves columns by variable id, so it is layout-robust) and re-run.

docs.title: 4.3 Back-cast / ground-truth canaries (MATLAB)
docs.text:
pipeline/_verify/gt.m recomputes the canonical conditional-forecast ground truth directly from the deployed app/public/data/bvar/US/*.json via conforekf.m; compare against the app's conditional output to confirm the scale conventions still hold after re-estimation.

matlab -batch "run('pipeline/_verify/gt.m')"

Then the data-pack gate (from app/): npm run data:verify (verify_cutoffs + pack-verify --full, which re-hashes every file and checks the dating against the estimation panels).

Done = tsc clean, all vitest green, build succeeds, verify_gvar24 all PASS, data:verify OK.

docs.title: 5. Deploy
docs.text:
The deploy target is the bvarscenario remote (matyasfarkas/BVARScenarioTool). A push to its main triggers a GitHub Action (.github/workflows/deploy-to-website.yml, on push to main touching app/**) that runs npm ci && npm run build (with BASE_PATH=/bvar-scenario), then copies app/out/* into the matyasfarkas/starter-hugo-academic website repo's static/bvar-scenario/. That repo is a Hugo Academic site published to GitHub Pages (note the netlify.toml trigger), which rebuilds and serves it at the /bvar-scenario path. (This workflow has no Hugo step itself; it only copies app/out.) The second site, gmapsmodel.com, is built by Netlify from the gmapsmodel remote (gmapsmodel/GMAPS) — push the same commit there too.

Do not push without explicit confirmation. Pushing to bvarscenario main is a deploy. Confirm the gate is green first.

cd "<repo root>"
git add app/public/data pipeline/country_rawdata pipeline/euro_redesign_staging pipeline/vintages
git commit -m "Re-estimate GVAR + members (data through <quarter>, pack <pack id>)"
git push bvarscenario HEAD:main     # Action copies app/out → starter-hugo-academic → Hugo rebuilds & serves on GitHub Pages
git push gmapsmodel HEAD:main       # Netlify → gmapsmodel.com

Hugo is pinned to 0.122.0 in the starter-hugo-academic repo (0.123+ removed getCSV and broke the theme — do not bump it); that pin lives in the website repo, not in this workflow.

Verify live. On both sites, <site>/data/manifest.json must show the new packId; then open the app and confirm a US baseline, a quick conditioning scenario, and the fiscal debt/GDP projection all look sane.

docs.title: 6. End-to-end (copy-paste skeleton) — pre-2026 path
docs.text:
For the current procedure use the ★ section at the top and the scripts in docs/reest-2026/runs/. This skeleton is the older path (six fiscal builders, sig6 port of every bloc, a 2026Q1 shift after the export) and is kept for reference.

# from <repo root>
# 1. GVAR-EM re-estimation (hours, 38 blocs) — validate on a subset first
US_ENDOGENOUS=1 \
  GVAR_WEIGHTS_FILE="$PWD/app/public/data/bvar/gvar/weights_full_38.json" \
  GVAR_DUMMY_BLOCS="CL CN CO CR EA ID IL IN IS JP KR MX NO TR UK ZA HK PE" \
  matlab -batch "run('pipeline/export_bvar_gvar24_loop.m')"

# 2. Fiscal SFA = exact residual (auto closure gate < 1e-6 each)
cd pipeline
for cc in us ea jp uk ca cn; do python3 "build_fiscal_${cc}_4var.py"; done
cd ..

# 3. Port (6 sig-figs) + swap runtime weights (if bloc set grew) + fiscal_meta + RE-INDEX + coupling + manifest
python3 pipeline/port_gvar_exports.py
cp app/public/data/bvar/gvar/weights_full_38.json app/public/data/bvar/gvar/weights_24bloc.json   # ONLY on a 33->38 change
for cc in US EA JP UK CA CN; do cp "pipeline/fiscal_meta/$cc.json" "app/public/data/bvar/$cc/fiscal_meta.json"; done
node pipeline/fix_fiscal_meta_indices.mjs   # MANDATORY: re-resolve fiscal idx by id (stale-index guard)
cd app
npx vite-node scripts/precompute_gvar_coupling.mjs   # vite-node, NOT node; dim -> 2360 at 38 blocs
node scripts/build_coverage_manifest.mjs             # rebuild coverage/provenance manifest

# 3b. MODEL UPDATE + 2026Q1 rebase — dates the re-exported histories, re-stamps + verifies the pack, then shifts:
npm run data:model-update -- --then-shift
# (the two steps it runs for the shift, for reference:)
npx vite-node scripts/refresh-quarter.mjs --bloc US --asof 2026Q1 --accept-revisions   # exact flags/order: data-refresh-rollout.md
npx vite-node scripts/nowcast_complete.mjs --to 2026Q1 --write --baselines

# 4. Gate
NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=8192 npx tsx scripts/verify_gvar24.mjs
npx tsc --noEmit && npx vitest run && BASE_PATH=/bvar-scenario npm run build
cd ..

# 5. Deploy (ONLY after the gate is green and confirmed)
git add app/public/data/bvar pipeline/fiscal_meta pipeline/country_rawdata
git commit -m "Re-estimate GVAR + fiscal block (data through <quarter>)"
git push bvarscenario main

docs.title: GMAPS 4.0 — Update Manual
docs.text:
How to keep GMAPS current: data updates, model updates, and new app versions. For two readers: users of the desktop app (sections 1–3) and the maintainer who produces updates (sections 4–9). Section 10 is a reference.

Applies to GMAPS 4.0.0 and later. Last revised 2026-10-08. The websites run data pack 2026Q2-reest-20261008b (data through 2026Q2, the genuine-data model update of October 2026); the 4.0.0 desktop installer carries 2026Q1-20261006 (section 7.4).

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
1. What changed in 4.0, in one page
  2. Installing GMAPS 4.0.0
  3. Updating the data on your computer (users)
  4. The ideas behind updates (maintainer)
  5. Monthly: is an update due?
  6. Quarterly: the data shift
  7. Yearly: the model update (re-estimation)
  8. Releasing a new app version
  9. When something fails
  10. Reference

docs.title: 1. What changed in 4.0, in one page
docs.text:
The data and the model are now separate from the app. Everything GMAPS shows (histories, forecasts, estimated models, uncertainty draws, trade weights) lives in a data pack: a folder of files plus one manifest.json that lists every file with its SHA-256 fingerprint and size. The app checks every file against that list before using it, and refuses a damaged or mismatched file. A problem with the pack as a whole (wrong version, an update made for another release, an unreadable manifest) stops the app with a full-screen message. A single damaged file found later is named in a red banner at the bottom of the screen, and whatever depends on it is not shown (a country's charts, or the whole global model). It never shows a wrong number.

That separation means:

  • New data does not need a new app. The maintainer sends an update pack (a small zip); users unzip it into a folder and press Reload.
  • A model update does not need a new app either, as long as the variables stay the same.
  • The dates come from the data itself. Each country's history file records the quarter of its first row (firstQuarter); the last quarter is always first quarter + number of rows − 1. There is no date setting that can drift out of step with the data.

Why the last point matters (what went wrong in September 2026). Two model updates (22 and 23 September) replaced each country's data with fresh model exports. A model export ends at the estimation end, 2025Q4. The July data shift had added 2026Q1, and that row was silently lost. But a separate date setting still said "2026Q1". For about two weeks, the US, the euro area, Japan, the UK and 31 other economies were shown one quarter late, the 15 seasonal economies had their quarterly pattern applied one quarter off, and the published 2026Q1 data were missing. Nothing failed, because the only check that compared rows with dates ran after a data shift, never after a model update.

4.0 fixes the cause, not just the symptom:

  • the date is computed from the data (no label to forget);
  • after every model update one command dates the new exports from the estimation panels and re-applies the data shift (npm run data:model-update -- --then-shift);
  • an offline calendar check compares the dated rows with the estimation panels the models were fitted on. It runs on every build and refuses to ship a mis-dated pack.

docs.title: Windows (x64)
docs.text:
1. Get GMAPS_4.0.0_x64-setup.exe (536 MB; or the no-install GMAPS_4.0.0_x64-portable.exe, 530 MB) from the release page, and compare its SHA-256 with SHA256SUMS.txt (PowerShell: Get-FileHash .\GMAPS_4.0.0_x64-setup.exe). The data built into 4.0.0 run to 2026Q1 (data pack 2026Q1-20261006). The websites already show the October 2026 model update (data to 2026Q2); see section 7.4 for how it reaches the desktop app.
  2. Double-click it. Windows SmartScreen may warn that the app is unrecognised (it is not code-signed). Click More info → Run anyway.
  3. GMAPS needs Microsoft Edge WebView2, which is part of Windows 10/11. On an older or stripped-down machine without it, install the "Evergreen WebView2 Runtime" from Microsoft.

Windows on a Mac (Parallels/UTM on Apple silicon). That Windows is the ARM edition. It runs the x64 app through Windows' built-in x64 emulation. That works, but it is slower than a native build. A native ARM64 Windows build can be made on request.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text: Build it on a Mac from the repository (cd app && npm install && npm run tauri build), or use a .dmg if one is provided. The app is unsigned: the first time, right-click → Open.

docs.title: Where the app keeps its data folder
docs.text:
System Data folder (created by Open data folder) Windows C:\Users\<you>\AppData\Roaming\io.github.matyasfarkas.gmaps\gmaps-data macOS ~/Library/Application Support/io.github.matyasfarkas.gmaps/gmaps-data Linux ~/.local/share/io.github.matyasfarkas.gmaps/gmaps-data

You never need to type these: Settings → Data pack → Open data folder creates and opens it.

docs.title: 3. Updating the data on your computer (users)
3.1 See which data you have
docs.text:
Open Settings (bottom left) → Data pack. It shows the pack name, how recent the data are ("data through 2026Q1"), and where they come from:

  • bundled with the app: the data that came with your installation;
  • update pack (data folder): an update you installed. The line also says how many files came from the update and how many from the built-in data;
  • external pack (data folder): a complete pack you installed.

docs.title: 3.2 Install an update pack
docs.text:
You receive a file such as 2026Q2-20261115_for_4.0.0.zip. The part after for_ is the app version it is made for.

  1. Settings → Data pack → Open data folder.
  2. Extract the contents of the zip into that folder, so that manifest.json sits directly in it (not in a sub-folder). On Windows, "Extract All" proposes a new sub-folder named after the zip. Either change the destination to the data folder itself, or move the extracted files up one level afterwards. If an older update is already there, let the new files replace the old ones.
  3. Press Reload (in the same panel). The Data pack line should now show the new pack and the new "data through" quarter.

The app checks the whole update before showing anything: - every file it ships, and every file it reuses from your built-in data, must match its fingerprint; - an update made for a different app version is refused, with a message that names the version it needs.

docs.title: 3.3 Go back to the built-in data
docs.text: Delete or rename manifest.json in the data folder, then press Reload. Nothing else is needed; the other files there are ignored.

docs.title: 3.4 Messages and what to do
docs.text:
What you see What it means What to do "This update pack (…) was built for the data pack X, but the data built into this app is pack Y" The update is for a different app version Ask for the update for your version, or a full pack "… could not be read from the data folder — the pack copied there looks incomplete" A file of the update is missing Extract the zip again, completely, into the data folder itself "… sha256 mismatch …" (red banner at the bottom of the screen) A file was changed or damaged Extract again; if it persists, ask for a new pack "This data pack requires the tool to be at least vX" The data need a newer app Install the newer app version

In every case you can go back to the built-in data (3.3).

docs.title: 4. The ideas behind updates (maintainer)
docs.text:
Term Meaning Data pack app/public/data/: all data files + manifest.json (fingerprint, size, and the dating of every country). The web build serves it; the desktop app has it built in. Calendar firstQuarter in each bvar/<C>/historical_levels.json. Last quarter = firstQuarter + rows − 1. The only source of dates. Panel quarter The common last quarter of the 35 coupled GVAR economies (they share one row grid). The 17 euro members follow it. Data shift Within the year: add the newly published quarter (US observed; other published values pinned; the rest nowcast through the model and shown in amber). The estimated model is frozen. Model update Once a year: re-estimate (MATLAB) and re-export. Changes the model fingerprint. Update pack Only the files that changed against the pack built into a released app version, plus a full manifest. One per recorded release. Release record pipeline/released_packs/<version>.manifest.json: the manifest of the pack built into that app version. Needed to cut update packs for it. Model fingerprint Hash of all GVAR companion_mean.json files. Unchanged by a data shift, changed by a model update. Archived vintages carry it, so the /monitor page knows whether a comparison is a pure data change.

Golden rules

  1. Never edit dates by hand. There is nothing to edit; the data carry their own calendar.
  2. After every model export, date and verify it before anything ships (section 7). The calendar check must pass.
  3. Never hand-edit a shipped data file to "fix" a value. Re-run the step that produces it.
  4. Pushing to main deploys the websites. Commit and push are always a deliberate human step; no script does them.
  5. Never fill a missing value. A quarter that is not published stays missing: the model draws it, and the app shows it in amber as a model estimate. The data list every such cell (estimation_mask.json, nowcast provenance, coverage flags).
  6. Never regenerate a pack under an existing pack id. Any change after pack-build gets a new id; an old id with new contents would turn every cached copy into a fingerprint error.

docs.title: 5. Monthly: is an update due?
docs.text:
cd app
npm run data:check

It asks the release calendars (FRED, OECD via DBnomics) for the latest quarter of a small set of sentinel series (US, euro area, Japan, Korea, China GDP; the US 10-year yield) and compares it with the panel quarter.

Exit Meaning Next step 0 Nothing new for every sentinel yet Nothing 10 A new quarter is published for every sentinel: a data shift is available Section 6 11 A full new calendar year is published beyond the model's estimation end: a model update is due Section 7

A GitHub Action (.github/workflows/data-check.yml) runs this on the 5th of every month and fails on purpose (so GitHub emails the repository owner) when 10 or 11 comes back. It never changes data.

docs.title: 6.1 One command
docs.text:
cd app
npm run data:shift -- --asof 2026Q2            # dry run: every gate, nothing written
npm run data:shift -- --asof 2026Q2 --commit   # the real run

Or let the scheduler do it: npm run data:auto checks and, if a shift is due, runs it with --commit (exit 0 nothing due, 10 shift done, 11 model update due, 1 error). It never commits or pushes. Example crontab line (6:00 on the 5th of each month):

0 6 5 * *  cd /path/to/repo/app && npm run data:auto >> ~/gmaps-auto.log 2>&1

docs.title: 6.2 What the shift does, step by step
docs.text: # Step Writes — Pre-flight: the at-rest dating is coherent (every history has a calendar; coverage + pack manifest agree). Stops otherwise. nothing 0 Archive the current data as a vintage (pipeline/vintages/<quarter>_shipped[_<model>]) archive 1 Counterfactual: the old data completed to the new quarter with no new information (the /monitor baseline) archive 2 US: append the observed quarter from FRED (gated; revisions accepted and logged) US history 2.5 Realized pins: every other published value for the new quarter (FRED mirrors of Eurostat, ECB, BoE, BoJ …), each gated against the shipped overlap pipeline/realized_pins_<q>.json 3 Cross-economy nowcast: one coupled model solve fills every remaining gap (flagged model-implied → amber in the charts) staging 4 Publish staging into app/public/data histories, forecasts 5 Euro members follow the euro area (skipped for a member already at the quarter) member histories 6 Re-simulate the uncertainty bands from the posterior draws (seeded) bands 7 Coverage manifest (dates from the data; the expected quarter is asserted) coverage_manifest.json 8 Release-impact record for /monitor release_impact.json 9 Vintage-comparison artifacts for /monitor vintages/ 10 Re-stamp the data pack (manifest.json, pack id <quarter>-<yyyymmdd>) manifest.json 11 Verification gate: dating coherent everywhere, every economy on the new quarter, no empty last-row cells, nowcast converged, every file re-hashed, calendar check nothing — stops on any problem 12 One update pack per recorded app release → packs/<pack>_for_<version>.zip packs/

docs.title: 6.3 After the run (deliberate)
docs.text:
1. npm test — the full test suite.
  2. npm run build — its prebuild re-verifies the whole pack (pack-verify --full).
  3. Look at /monitor and a few charts: the history should end at the new quarter, the first forecast quarter should be the one after it, and amber dashed tails mark model-implied values.
  4. git add app/public/data pipeline/vintages pipeline/realized_pins_<q>.json && git commit
  5. When you decide to update the websites: push to main (this deploys).
  6. Send the update pack(s) from packs/ to desktop users (section 3.2). A quarterly data shift changes few files: the 2025Q4 → 2026Q1 shift (Oct 2026) produced an update pack of 297 files, 3.1 MB zipped.

docs.title: 6.4 If it stops half-way
docs.text: Every step is safe to repeat. Re-run the same --commit command; finished work is skipped or harmlessly redone. To undo a run completely: git checkout -- app/public/data (and remove the new pipeline/vintages/* folders) — there is no date to restore.

docs.title: 7. Yearly: the model update (re-estimation)
docs.text:
When data:check returns 11 (normally in Q2, once the previous year is fully published):

cd app
npm run data:q1prep -- --year 2026     # confirms the year is published; prints the runbook

The October 2026 update is the worked example. The scripts it ran are in docs/reest-2026/runs/ (with a README giving the order), the method decisions in docs/reest-2026/PLAN.md, and the review in docs/reest-2026/REVIEW.md. Each MATLAB setting is explained in docs/REESTIMATING_MODELS.md.

docs.title: 7.1 Data
docs.text:
1. Rebuild every economy's panel from its source registry (pipeline/sources/registry/), using genuine data only, to the latest published quarter. Unpublished cells stay missing (golden rule 5).
  2. Rebuild what is derived from the data: the fiscal stock-flow adjustment and the euro-member panels (docs/reest-2026/RECIPE_live_model.md §3, step 0).

docs.title: 7.2 Estimation (MATLAB)
docs.text:
1. The 35 coupled economies: pipeline/export_bvar_gvar24_loop.m with BVAR_DIFF_GP=1 US_ENDOGENOUS=1 NDRAWS=1000 MAXIT=30 BVAR_SEED=1 GVAR_FIXHYPER=1 GVAR_NOFILL=1 (runs/run_gvar35b.sh). It iterates until the foreign ("star") variables stop changing. In 2026 it converged at sweep 6, after about 1 h 40 min on a 4-core machine.
  2. GVAR_NOFILL=1: missing cells at the start, in the middle and at the end stay missing, and the sampler draws them. The export lists them in estimation_mask.json.
  3. GVAR_FIXHYPER=1 with BVAR_SEED: every sweep uses the same random numbers. Without this, sweeps are not comparable and the loop does not converge.
  4. The 17 euro members: pipeline/export_bvar_euro_redesign.m for each member, with BVAR_DIFF_GP=1 GVAR_NOFILL=1 CGL_FIXED_COMPANION=1 (runs/run_members.sh). A re-run gives identical results.

docs.title: 7.3 Into the data pack (run in app/ unless shown otherwise)
docs.text:
1. Port. Copy the 35 GVAR exports raw, including estimation_mask.json. Port the members with pipeline/port_gvar_exports.py. Then run node pipeline/fix_fiscal_meta_indices.mjs and node pipeline/fix_external_meta_indices.mjs. They re-find the fiscal and external column positions by variable name. In 2026, adding a deflator column moved them (runs/port_to_app.sh).
  2. Date. Run node scripts/stamp_calendar.mjs, then npx vite-node scripts/build_coverage_manifest.mjs --panel-quarter <Q>.
  3. Coupling. Run npx vite-node scripts/precompute_gvar_coupling.mjs. ρ(M) must be below 1 (2026: 0.9719).
  4. Ragged edge. Run npx vite-node scripts/nowcast_complete.mjs --write --baselines --out <dir>, check that it converged, and publish the coupled economies from <dir> (runs/stageA.sh).
  5. Members and debt. Run apply_member_completion.mjs, then roll_d0_forward.mjs. The second rolls debt starting points forward to the panel quarter and keeps the published value as d0_observed.
  6. Forecasts, bands, draws. Run regen_gr_baselines_via_loader.mjs and regen_gvar_bands.mjs, then node scripts/gzip_companion_draws.mjs.
  7. Pack.
    • Run build_coverage_manifest.mjs --panel-quarter <Q> and vintages_publish.mjs.
    • Stamp the pack under a new id: node scripts/pack-build.mjs --pack-id <Q>-reest-<yyyymmdd>.
    • Verify: node scripts/verify_cutoffs.mjs --allow-ragged --dating-only, then npx vite-node scripts/pack-verify.mjs --full (runs/stageB.sh).
  8. Review. Run npm test and npm run build. Compare old and new (docs/reest-2026/compare_old_new.py). Open the built site in a browser. Commit; push only when you decide to.

The steps above apply when the panels already end at the latest published quarter, as in 2026: the model is fitted to the latest data. If the exports end earlier (a model estimated to a year end), run npm run data:model-update -- --then-shift instead of steps 6 and 8, after step 7. It dates each export from its estimation panel; a country it cannot place stops the run, and nothing is guessed. It then re-stamps and verifies the pack, and shifts the panel to the latest published quarter.

docs.title: 7.4 Getting a model update to desktop users
docs.text:
A model update changes most files (every model and every band file), so its update pack is large: hundreds of MB, mostly the uncertainty draws. Also check whether the new data rely on app code newer than the installed version.

The October 2026 pack relies on two display changes made after 4.0.0: every effective exchange rate is shown as an index level, and interior model-estimated quarters get amber marks. The 4.0.0 app accepts the pack (minToolVersion is 4.0.0), but it would show those two things the old way. A new app version (section 8) is the clean route. If you send an update pack instead, tell users about that difference.

Status on 2026-10-08: neither has been done. Desktop users have 2026Q1-20261006.

docs.title: 8. Releasing a new app version
docs.text:
1. Set the version in app/package.json, app/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json and app/src-tauri/Cargo.toml (all three the same). If the data now need a feature of this version, raise MIN_TOOL_VERSION in app/scripts/pack-build.mjs and re-run it (pack-verify check [4] guarantees a pack never requires a newer app than the one it ships with).
  2. Make sure app/public/data is final and verified: npm run data:verify.
  3. Record the release (needed so future data shifts can cut update packs for it): node scripts/pack-record-release.mjs --version 4.0.0 → commit pipeline/released_packs/4.0.0.manifest.json.
  4. Build:
  5. Web: npm run build (the website deploy does this in CI on push to main).
  6. Windows x64 (cross-compiled on the Linux workstation): see app/src-tauri/README.md ("Windows x64 — cross-compiled from Linux"): npm run build:tauri, then XWIN_ACCEPT_LICENSE=1 npx tauri build --runner cargo-xwin --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc --bundles nsis, then run makensis on the generated script with NSISDIR set (Tauri's own Linux NSIS step ignores it).
  7. macOS: on a Mac, npm run tauri build.
  8. Publish the installers (GitHub Release on the private repository) with their SHA-256 checksums.

docs.title: 9. When something fails
docs.text: Message Cause Fix pre-flight FAILED — fix the at-rest dating first The coverage or pack manifest disagree with the data's calendars (e.g. files were replaced without re-stamping) npm run data:model-update … history has no calendar (stamp it …) A freshly exported history without firstQuarter npm run data:model-update cannot place its history on the calendar No history row equals the country's estimation panel at its last quarter: the export and the panel do not belong together Check that the export is from that panel; only with independent evidence: node scripts/stamp_calendar.mjs --first <Q> --blocs <C> MISDATED — the row dated X equals the panel at Y The calendar is wrong for that country Find out why (wrong firstQuarter?) and fix; never ship the coupled GVAR blocs do not share one last quarter Some coupled economies were shifted and others not Re-run the shift, or the model update coverage_manifest.json says … but the data end … The coverage manifest is stale npx vite-node scripts/build_coverage_manifest.mjs (or data:model-update) pack-verify … sha256 mismatch / listed but missing on disk A data file changed after the pack was stamped, or is missing Re-run node scripts/pack-build.mjs after the intended change; restore an unintended one pack needs tool ≥ X but this tool is Y MIN_TOOL_VERSION is above the app version Lower it, or release the newer app The web build fails in prebuild pack-verify --full found a mismatch (the deploy refuses to ship data the app would refuse) As above

docs.title: Commands (run in app/)
docs.text: Command What it does npm run data:check Is a shift (10) or a model update (11) due? npm run data:shift -- --asof <Q> [--commit] The quarterly data shift (dry run without --commit) npm run data:auto Unattended: run a due shift (--commit); exit 0/10/11/1 npm run data:model-update [-- --then-shift] After a re-export: date, re-stamp, verify (then shift) npm run data:q1prep -- --year <YYYY> Re-estimation readiness + runbook npm run data:verify verify_cutoffs + pack-verify --full node scripts/stamp_calendar.mjs --check Every country's calendar + calendar-check verdict npm run pack:build Re-stamp manifest.json npm run pack:verify -- [--full] [--dir <update> --bundled <built-in>] Verify a full or an update pack npm run pack:delta -- --base <manifest> --out <dir> --zip Cut an update pack by hand npm run pack:record-release -- --version <x.y.z> Record a released app's built-in pack

docs.title: What the checks guarantee
docs.text:
• pack-verify --full (also in every web build): every listed file exists, has its recorded size and SHA-256; no unused plain twin of a .gz is listed; the GVAR weights match the coupling they were made with; the pack does not require a newer app than its own; the dating in the manifest equals each history's calendar; the calendar check confirms the dating against the estimation panels.
  • verify_cutoffs (end of every shift): every history has a calendar; all economies end at the panel quarter; the coverage and pack manifests agree with the calendars; no empty cells in the last row; the nowcast converged.
  • In the app: the data are refused with a full-screen message if the pack is incompatible, an update was cut for a different version, or any file fails its fingerprint.

docs.title: Files
docs.text: File Role app/public/data/manifest.json The pack: version fields, panel quarter, per-country dating, every file's fingerprint app/public/data/coverage_manifest.json Per-variable coverage, sources, flags (drives the Data & coverage page and the amber tails) app/public/data/bvar/<C>/historical_levels.json History (100·log for log variables) + firstQuarter app/scripts/lib/calendar.mjs Calendar arithmetic + the calendar check pipeline/vintages/ Archived vintages for /monitor (each with vintage_meta.json: origin, kind, model fingerprint) pipeline/released_packs/ Built-in manifests of released app versions packs/ (not in git) Update packs to send

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• The list of countries is still compiled into the app: a pack can update existing countries but not add one.
  • Files are fingerprinted one by one; the manifest itself is not yet signed (the format leaves room for it).
  • There is no "import zip" button: users extract the zip into the data folder.
  • The app still contains a build-time copy of the trade weights and of six economies' model descriptions (gvarSolve.ts). They are start-up defaults only. Once the pack loads, the app uses the pack's own, fingerprinted weights (if the pack lists weights that fail to load, the global model stops; it does not fall back), and the list of countries comes from the compiled roster (first point above).
  • Fixed in October 2026: a file that failed its fingerprint check after start-up used to reach only the browser console (the global model then left that country out, and the weights fell back to the build-time copy). Now every such failure is named in a red banner, the country shows an error panel instead of charts, and the global model refuses to load from a partial set.
  • A within-year shift re-syncs only the previous quarter to the latest source vintage. After a large source revision, the quarter before keeps the older vintage, so the growth rate across that seam mixes vintages. (Example, now resolved: after the US annual revision of Sep 2026, US 2025Q4 GDP growth showed 1.6% annualised against 0.2% on current data. The October 2026 rebuild took every series from its current vintage, and the data now show 0.2%.)
  • Resolved in October 2026: the euro members had run an older model generation. They were re-estimated with the rest, in growth rates.

docs.title: Global Macroeconomic Analysis Projections and Scenarios — Quick Start
docs.text:
This tool shows you quarterly forecasts for 52 economies — growth, inflation, interest rates, public finances, and more — and lets you bend them. Click on a chart where you think inflation will be, and every other chart updates so the whole forecast stays consistent with the estimated economics. Everything runs in your browser; nothing to install.

This page is the five-minute walk-through. The complete manual is the User Manual (PDF): each section states a method with its exact implemented conventions and then shows how to operate it from the interface, with worked Examples that name the on-screen controls. When this page and the manual disagree, trust the manual.

docs.title: Three rules that govern everything you see
docs.text:
1. Data are data. Solid history is observed. Where a country's latest quarter has not been published yet, the model estimates it from everything already observed elsewhere — those model estimates are always drawn as an amber dashed tail, never disguised as data. A quarter missing inside the history (for example US inflation in 2025 Q4, when October 2025 was not published) gets an open amber marker.
  2. The model is estimated once a year, then frozen. New data releases shift the starting point of the forecast within the year but never silently change the model. Re-estimation happens once a year, after the previous year is fully published, on all data published so far. The data now run through 2026 Q2. The Monitor page (top bar) shows what each data release did to the forecasts.
  3. Judgment is visible. If you move a forecast away from what the model says — a scenario, a long-run target, a policy counterfactual — the chart says so.

docs.title: Your first scenario in five minutes
docs.text:
1. Open the tool and pick a country. The Country dropdown in the top bar reads United States by default. The GVAR group in that dropdown lists the economies linked into the cross-country system; everything under Other countries moves on its own. Leave Units on q/q ann. (quarter-on-quarter, annualised) and Uncertainty on None.

2. Read one chart before touching anything. On the Inflation chart: history sits on a lightly shaded background (solid line = observed data); the forecast is the dotted line labelled Baseline, wrapped in the model's own faint grey fan. The first forecast quarter is labelled NC — short for nowcast, the model's estimate of the current, not-yet-published quarter. If a series' latest quarters are amber and dashed, the model filled them in — they are flagged, not data.

3. Bend the policy rate. On the Policy Rate chart, click the small condition button in its header — it turns blue and reads CONDITIONED. Press the mouse down on the forecast part of the chart about four quarters in, drag half a percentage point above the dotted baseline, release. (Shortcut: right-clicking an unconditioned chart conditions it and plants the point where you clicked, in one go.) A dot marks the quarter you pinned; only that quarter is imposed — the model fills in the most plausible route through your point.

4. Watch the rest of the economy respond. Scroll the grid: every chart has updated, not just the one you touched. With a tighter rate path, growth typically cools and inflation eases with a lag. Read it as "what usually accompanies a higher rate," not "what the rate causes" — for true cause-and-effect, use the policy counterfactual (manual §9). Other countries have not moved: cross-border spillovers are off until you switch them on (§5).

5. Put uncertainty bands around it. In the top bar set Uncertainty to Quick and press Compute. A shaded band in the scenario's colour wraps your scenario's solid coloured line on every chart — the middle two-thirds of plausible outcomes. It pinches shut at the quarter you dragged: you imposed that value, so there is no uncertainty about it there. Full does the same with 200 draws.

6. Ask which shocks would have produced it. Once a scenario moves anything, a Drivers button with an amber exp badge appears above the chart grid, in the same action row as ▶ Solve full GVAR. It opens a panel on the right that reads your scenario through a dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) model taken from the Macroeconomic Model Base, and reports which sequence of that model's own structural shocks would have produced the path you are looking at, over the first twelve forecast quarters.

With no clicks on the United States it opens on Smets–Wouters (2007), watching all seven of that model's observables and naming all seven of its shocks. The answer is drawn as stacked contributions in three classes — Monetary, Demand, Supply — anchored on the baseline in the same units as the main chart, with a grey Residual (unexplained) band for anything the named shocks cannot reproduce, and a 100 % shares strip underneath. The Contributions to dropdown switches which observable you are reading. On other countries the four extra observables are not in the data, so the panel runs on output, inflation and the policy rate alone, Classes is greyed out, and Groups gives one series per shock instead.

Read it as a conditional statement rather than a diagnosis. It says which mix of this model's shocks reproduces the path, not what caused it, and a different model gives a different mix. The feature is experimental, and what has been checked is that the decomposition recovers a shock sequence the same model generated — never that the labels are the right ones for the world.

7. Clean up. In the left control panel, click Reset at the top of the Scenario section (clears the active scenario for the current country only), and set Uncertainty back to None. You are back at the model's own view.

docs.title: Where to go next in the manual
docs.text:
Section What it covers §2 Getting started The screen, reading one chart, the walk-through above in full §3–4 The models and conditioning Estimation, hard and soft pins, cookbook recipes, outside forecasts, uncertainty bands §5 The global model Cross-border transmission: switch it on and let a US scenario reach the euro area, Japan, and China §6–7 Public finances and external accounts Revenue, spending, deficits, debt, and the net-foreign-assets (NFA) block §8 Long-run anchors Set where a variable settles in the long run (per-variable vs joint solve) §9 Policy counterfactuals The true policy experiment: what a different rate path would have caused §10 Scenario drivers Step 6 in full: what the decomposition solves, and where its class view is and is not licensed §11 Data, vintages, and updates Sources, the amber nowcast tails, the Monitor page

The same sections carry the machinery in full — Bayesian VAR (BVAR) estimation, the state space and Kalman smoother, the GVAR coupling, the fiscal accounting, long-run anchors, data, evaluation, and reproducibility — each stated next to the controls that operate it.

Two pages outside the manual go further on step 6. Drivers Decomposition Methodology states what the panel solves, the two rules that keep the reading honest (name no more shocks than observables you are watching, and read collinear shocks jointly), and the single configuration in which the Monetary/Demand/Supply split is licensed. The Scenario Cookbook works the panel end to end on its credit-crunch recipe.

docs.title: Consensus-anchor review — July 2026
docs.text: Outcome: the shipped default anchor set shrinks from 104 anchors across 46 blocs to 32 anchors across 23 blocs. Every kept anchor fixes a genuine long-run pathology and leaves the near-term forecast inside the economy's own historical experience; everything else is dropped — either because the model already lands at consensus, or because the correction did more damage than the bias it corrected. The pruning was adversarially verified: three independent agents re-derived every sampled verdict exactly from the shipped files, and a referee pass found (and we fixed) three false drops and two blind spots before shipping.

docs.title: Why anchors exist — and why they are not innocuous
docs.text:
The companions are estimated on short samples of highly persistent data. Near the unit root, autoregressive coefficients are biased downward in finite samples (Hurwicz/Kendall bias), and in a VAR with an intercept the level must be carried by something: the constant absorbs it, so the implied unconditional mean — the model's long-run terminal — is biased upward. The shipped terminals show it plainly (US deflator terminal 4.3 against 2.0 consensus; US nominal growth ≈ 8, which made the debt ratio melt away at i−g ≈ −3.9).

The consensus anchors correct that bias — but the correction (δc) is a rigid translation of the whole path, not a change in dynamics. A large terminal gap buys anchor exactness with a front-loaded near-term shift (the July 2026 episode: the joint solve pushed displayed US inflation negative for two forecast years). Correcting the upward bias is not innocuous, so the shipped set must be the minimum that resolves the worst pathologies without breaking the forecast. The full fix for the bias itself is the annual re-estimation (stationarity-inducing priors on the offending equations — the exact precedent is the FREV/FPEXP/SFA→WN prior fix), not translation.

docs.title: The smell battery
docs.text:
Engine: app/scripts/anchor_smell.mjs — replicates the app's exact pipeline (buildDriftCache → SENS guard → computeDriftDeltaFull, per-variable mode = the shipping default, H = 20). Per anchor:

Test Fires when REDUNDANT |target − model terminal| < 0.75 pp (growth/inflation), 0.5 (EFFI), 1.0 (fiscal shares) SIGN_FLIP baseline first-2y stays ≥ +0.25 but the anchored path dips < −0.25 (growth/inflation) LOW/HIGH_WINDOW the anchored first-2y leaves the COVID-masked history envelope ± 0.5 σ and deepens/exceeds the baseline's own extreme by > 1 pp (the AND-gate tolerates NSA-seasonal dips; the COVID mask keeps the fence meaningful — unmasked, India's −110 COVID print made any dip "historical") EFFI_NEG the anchored effective interest rate goes negative anywhere in the window NC_JUMP the display shift at the first forecast quarter exceeds 2.5 pp NOT_EFFICACIOUS the anchored terminal fails to move toward the target (cross-drag dominates) CROSS_DRAG the anchor alone displaces an unanchored headline terminal (growth, inflation, EFFI) by > 1 pp

Per-variable δc contributions are additive across targets (verified to 2 × 10⁻¹⁴), so the cross-drag attribution is exact. Verdicts are iterated on the surviving set to a fixed point, then every harmful-dropped anchor gets one Pareto-safe re-admission trial against the final set (headline macro anchors tried before fiscal shares; a candidate enters only if the entire enlarged set survives re-judging). This matters: the flagship EA HICP anchor had been killed at iteration 0 purely by the cross-drag of co-candidates (EA EFFI/FREV) that themselves died in the same iteration; re-admission recovered it (its true path vs the final set: min −0.07, terminal 3.36 → 1.53, drag on unanchored EA variables ≤ 0.28). Re-admitted: EA HICP, US EFFI, CO GDP, PL HICP.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Kept: 32 anchors, 23 blocs. Headline keeps: US GDPH→2 + JGDP→2 + EFFI→5 (the flagship nominal-bias fix: nominal-growth terminal 8 → 4.3, fiscal snowball i−g −3.92 → −0.03); EA HICP→2 (terminal 3.36 → 1.53) + FPEXP→47; RU CPI→4 (model 6.55); IS CPI→2.5 (4.34); IN GDP→6.5 (8.07); SA CPI→4.5 (2.44); CR CPI→3 (0.91); UK EFFI→4 + FREV→40; CN GDP→4.3 + FREV→25.5; plus AT, BR, CA, CL, CO, FR, ID, IL, LU, MX, NO, PL, PT, TH.

Dropped redundant — the model already lands within threshold of consensus (AU, BE, DE, DK, SE, KR, NL, ES, …). An anchor that moves nothing adds only risk.

Dropped harmful — the correction broke the forecast. The worst offenders were exactly the blocs with the largest terminal pathologies: TR CPI (terminal 32 vs target 5), HU HICP (10.4), SK/LT/LV/SI HICP (4–7), CA/CZ/NZ/UK CPI, MY, FI, TW, GR. The referee's trim analysis (largest feasible partial correction λ) settled drop-vs-trim decisively: every feasible trim saturates the origin-jump guard — the 2.5 pp threshold becomes the shipped discontinuity — and for TR the maximal clean trim still leaves a 27 % terminal. A translation cannot fix these honestly. They are the priority queue for the Q1 re-estimation* (stationarity-inducing priors on the offending equations). Also documented: AR ships un-anchored with a residual growth-terminal pathology (0.04 vs 2.0 consensus) — its own-path-clean anchor was rejected because it alone drags unanchored AR CPI by 5.45 pp.

Fiscal snowball coherence (terminal i−g_nom, baseline → kept set): US −3.92 → −0.03, EA −3.22 → −1.04, UK −3.44 → −1.32, CN −3.21 → −1.73, CA −1.86 → −2.22. No sign flips; the US debt path is no longer driven by an 8 % nominal-growth terminal. Side effect accepted knowingly: UK keeps FREV while FPEXP fell to cross-drag, moving the terminal primary surplus from an implausible +3.3 to ≈ +0.3 pp of GDP — toward realism.

docs.title: Known accepted edges (documented, not hidden)
docs.text:
• IN GDP ships a soft first year (anchored NC ≈ 0.8 % for India) to fix an 8.07 → 6.5 terminal; the baseline's own NC (2.8) is itself implausible — India's near-term dynamics are a re-estimation item either way.
  • The kept US pair drags the unanchored US rate complex down (POLRATE −1.29 at terminal) — under the 1 pp headline bar for EFFI but visible; a set-cumulative, direction-aware cross-drag test is queued for the next review round, along with a primary-balance displacement gate and a spillover audit (kept δc's propagate to receiving blocs via the trend-spillover toggle, off by default).
  • NC_JUMP measures damage against the baseline origin; the honest yardstick is the nowcast (the baseline near-cast carries the same Hurwicz bias). Queued.
  • A ramped-δ engine variant (phase the correction in over ~8 quarters, zero at origin) would eliminate origin jumps as a category and could make TR/HU-class anchors shippable before re-estimation. Queued as a design option.

docs.title: What this means for users
docs.text:
• Most economies now ship fully model-driven — what you see is the estimate, judgment-free.
  • Where an anchor ships, it fixes a documented long-run bias and its whole path stays inside the economy's own (COVID-masked) historical experience.
  • The long-run-target panel is unchanged: any anchor can still be set manually, in either solve mode (per-variable default, joint opt-in).

Full machine-readable report: npx vite-node scripts/anchor_smell.mjs --json <out> from app/.

docs.text: Date of check: 2026-06-22 · Branch: improve-live · Mode: READ-ONLY availability probe (no data/code edited, nothing committed).

docs.title: Goal recap
docs.text: Extend the OBSERVED panel by one quarter (2025Q4 → 2026Q1) and let the forecast re-anchor from the new last-observed state. The model companion (companion_mean / companion_draws) stays fixed — same post-estimation philosophy as the δc long-run sliders. This note only answers: is 2026Q1 published yet, source-by-source, economy-by-economy?
