The regime banner reads rank 84/84, exact-fit, so no residual, collinearity or rank warning fires, and the residual band is flat at zero (Remark 1). To read the same decomposition for inflation instead we change the "Contributions to" dropdown; the solve does not change, because it uses all seven observables jointly and only the display picks one.

Example 2 (Decomposing on a bloc without the native columns). We switch the app to a non-US bloc and open Drivers. The lens is still US_SW07, but the five spec columns the native observables need are absent, so the budget is three and the named set is the greedy non-collinear three: interest_, fiscal_, ea. Classes is greyed with its tooltip, the view falls back to Groups, and the chart shows three per-shock series labelled Monetary (interest_), Government (fiscal_) and TFP (ea). The regime is 36/36, exact-fit. The caveat paragraph at the foot of the drawer gains the sentence explaining why Classes is unavailable. This is the honest reading available on that bloc: three shocks through a US lens, with no class aggregation behind it.

Example 3 (The FRB/US census lens and its cluster naming). We select "FRB/US linearised (2022, MMB) — 54-shock census" from the model picker. The drawer fetches a further 10.7 MB of impulse responses, then names the shipped default triple hqlfpr, interest_, pcer_l, which covers 19 of the 54 shocks. Groups shows one series per cluster, labelled by each cluster's largest member. We open the "Cluster membership" expander to see which shocks each composite column stands for, and read the bottom caveat, which states that this lens has no row in bench_simple_decomp.m and that the clusters are empirical, chained collinearity components rather than economic classes. If we then re-name the clusters by hand, an amber warning appears: only the shipped default naming carries a build-time recovery check, and most alternative triples fail it even though the rank test passes.

The controls fall into two groups. Always visible are the lens row (model title, any dropped-shock note, and a "Change model" link), the [Classes | Groups] toggle, the chart-view dropdown (Forecast, or Deviation from baseline), Reset, and Customize. Under Customize the drawer exposes:

  • Use all — watch every mappable observable, then name every unit the budget allows, skipping collinear duplicates.
  • Input source — "Scenario (displayed)" or "External forecast combination"; the latter is disabled and annotated when imports exist but the master switch is off, or when nothing is imported for this bloc.
  • Domestic | Global path — shown only for the scenario source, and only when both an isolated and a coupled path exist.
  • Observables — three locked chips with a padlock, plus the four addable native chips on the US bloc, each annotated with the fact that it raises the budget by one.
  • Measurement error — a strict-to-permissive slider shown only when native observables are added, displaying the current row weight \(w = 1/\sqrt{1+\mathrm{me}}\) with \(\mathrm{me} \in [0,4]\) and a default of 1.
  • Cluster chips — the cluster list for the two FRB/US lenses.
  • Experimental: raw shocks — a fold containing the raw/cluster switch and the raw shock chips.

Reset restores US_SW07 with its Use-all default, Classes, the scenario source and the follow-display chart view, and it overwrites the saved per-bloc model choice.

Remark 6 (The measurement-error slider does nothing at budget-max). At \(K = q\) the stacked system is square, so scaling both \(\Theta\) and \(z\) by a positive diagonal row weighting leaves the solution identical: \(W\Theta x = Wz \iff \Theta x = z\). In the default US configuration the slider is therefore rendered but disabled, and its tooltip says so and tells the user to un-name a shock if they want the added observables to have a role in the solve. The slider is real only in the underdetermined case.

Remark 7 (The delta view need not match the panel's units). The chart view auto-follows the main display: when the app is showing deviations from baseline the drawer opens in "Deviation from baseline", otherwise in "Forecast", and a manual choice then sticks. The delta chart's bars are always the panel's rate deviation, whereas the main panels' "% vs base" mode has a level sub-mode and defaults to level. Auto-follow can therefore put the drawer in different units from the panel that prompted it. The axis title always states the unit; read it before comparing magnitudes.

Remark 8 (The shares strip is a norm share, not a variance decomposition). For the selected observable, each series' share is the \(\ell^2\) norm of its contribution path divided by the sum of those norms plus the residual's, in percent. Shares therefore always sum to 100 and are never negative, which means the strip cannot display two contributions that offset each other as such. It is a magnitude summary, not a decomposition of forecast-error variance.

Warnings fire for the residual-able regime (with rank and rows shown), for named shocks that form a flagged collinear pair (with the measured \(\lvert\cos\rvert\)), for decomposing a path other than the one displayed (the Domestic/Global override is sticky, so this warning shows outside the collapsed fold), for the experimental raw-shock mode, for rank-deficient named columns, and for departing from the validated default naming on the FRB/US lenses. An index fetch failure is reported as an error; a per-model response-file failure is recorded and offers a Retry, which matters for the two ~10.7 MB FRB/US files.

docs.title: The data payload
docs.text:
The feature adds app/public/data/dsge/census/, containing the 36 KB index and eight census response files: CA_LS07 (47 KB), BRA_SAMBA08 (123 KB), EA_SW03 (200 KB), EA_SWW14 (217 KB), HK_FP13 (218 KB), UK_SM11 (231 KB), and the two FRB/US census files at 10.6 MB and 10.8 MB. Four further models are indexed rather than copied, since they already live in the irfs tree: US_SW07 (215 KB), US_CMR14 (1.8 MB), US_FRB08 (352 KB) and US_FRB22_mcap (407 KB). The SW07 and CMR14 files were regenerated by this feature to carry their full native shock sets; the interest_ and fiscal_ columns that the existing policy-counterfactual feature reads are unchanged to about \(5\times10^{-11}\) by that regeneration, which is re-export rounding.

The index is fetched once per session on the first drawer open, and a model's response file on selection, cached per model for the session. Both go through loadJSON, a plain fetch under ${NEXT_PUBLIC_BASE_PATH}/data/ with no client-side decompression. In practice the default lens costs 36 KB plus 215 KB; choosing either 54-shock FRB/US lens costs a further 10.7 MB.

The index carries schema: "gmaps-drivers-index/1", the build date, horizonQuarters (12, asserted equal to DRIVERS_H by the test suite), commonObservables, collinearThreshold (0.95), the verbatim shockClasses block, and one record per model. Each model record gives the site-absolute file path the drawer fetches and the repository source it came from; sha256 and sha256Source, which the test suite re-hashes against every shipped file; the usable shocks and the dropped list with a reason (zero-response or missing-observable); hasOutput; the collinearPairs with \(\cos\) rounded to six decimals; and, where applicable, an optional display title, sourceNote, menuHidden, classMapKey, clusters and defaultNamed. The full field list is in Data Schemas; the loader's types are at app/src/lib/data/loader.ts:96–160.

docs.title: Limits of the claim
docs.text:
The feature is experimental, and it is badged as such in the interface. Its claim is model-conditional: the decomposition answers what mix of model \(M\)'s structural shocks would have produced the displayed path. It does not say what caused the scenario, and it is not model-free shock labelling. An earlier attempt at a model-free validation failed its pre-committed gate; those numbers are unlicensed, are not part of this feature, and appear nowhere in the tool or its documentation.

What is validated is same-model recovery. Every number in simple_decomp_results.txt and class_recovery_results.txt comes from generating a path with a model's own known shock sequence and recovering it under that same model, so it measures the estimator, not the model, and not the world. A different lens gives a different answer, and the lenses are not equally validated. bench_simple_decomp.m ran exactly eight models — US_SW07, US_CMR14, EA_SW03, EA_SWW14, CA_LS07, HK_FP13, BRA_SAMBA08 and UK_SM11 — and never ran any FRB/US lens. The drawer's bottom caveat is therefore per-model: it cites the bench only for those eight, and for the others states that what backs the shipped default naming is a build-time recovery check rather than a bench row. That build-time scan exists for the two clustered FRB/US lenses. US_FRB08 has neither a bench row nor a build-time scan, and no document should assert one for it.

Aggregation into classes is the narrowest claim on the page, and it is licensed at one configuration only: US_SW07, all seven observables watched, all seven class-map shocks named. Un-naming a single shock revokes it (Remark 3). CMR14's families are that model's own class map used as an organising grouping and not a licensed class split (Remark 4), and the FRB/US clusters are an empirical grouping of response directions whose members are chained rather than mutually parallel (Remark 5). Of those clusters, only the shipped default naming carries a recovery check, and that check is a build-time scan rather than a bench: 123 of 1,771 possible triples pass for US_FRB22 and 122 of 1,330 for the VAR-expectations variant. Any other naming is exploratory. A full-rank \(\Theta\) is not evidence to the contrary, because conditioning is what decides whether a naming is usable and rank does not imply it.

Four smaller limits are worth carrying into any write-up. Where a pair of shocks is flagged collinear, the split within that pair is not identified and the pair must be read as one object (Remark 2). In the exact-fit regime the residual is zero by construction and is no evidence that the named shocks explain the path (Remark 1). The shares strip below the chart is a norm share and not a variance decomposition, so it cannot show two contributions offsetting each other (Remark 8). And the seven-observable mode exists only on the US bloc; every other bloc runs at three observables, where no configuration in the menu licenses a class view.

Finally, three numbers quoted in source comments do not reproduce under independent measurement and are deliberately absent from this page: a pair of SW07 column norms, an error range for a CMR14 collinear pair, and a failure magnitude for the FRB22 top-three-by-size triple. In each case the qualitative point holds and is stated above; the specific figure is not repeated.

docs.title: Regeneration
docs.text:
Example 4 (Rebuilding the shipped index and re-running the validation benches). We regenerate the index whenever the class maps, the census responses or the model menu change. The builder reads pipeline/census_irfs/MANIFEST.json, each census model's Taylor.json, the class maps, and the four irfs-tree response files; it writes the index and copies each census file into the public tree, refusing to ship any file whose sha256 does not match the manifest. We then re-run the two MATLAB benches, which print to stdout rather than writing files, so the committed transcripts under docs/paper/ are captured by redirection. Finally we run the licence tests, of which there are 26 across the three Drivers test files. The commands are as follows:

# 1. Rebuild the shipped index and the census copies (runs from anywhere in the repo).
node app/scripts/build_drivers_index.mjs

# 2. Re-run the two validation benches and capture their transcripts.
matlab -batch "run('pipeline/bench_simple_decomp.m')"  > docs/paper/simple_decomp_results.txt
matlab -batch "run('pipeline/bench_class_recovery.m')" > docs/paper/class_recovery_results.txt

# 3. Re-run the licence tests (26 across drivers-decomp{,-v2,-v3}.test.ts).
cd app && npm test

Two prerequisites are worth stating before anyone runs step 1 or step 2. The builder needs pipeline/census_irfs/, the 97-model census response tree, which is not present on the deployment branch; without it the script fails at its first read. bench_simple_decomp.m reads the shipped US_SW07 and US_CMR14 files plus the six census models' Taylor.json, and bench_class_recovery.m reads the class maps, those same two shipped files and US_FRB22_mcap/Taylor.json, so both benches run only in a checkout that carries the census tree. The public census/*.json copies are byte-identical to their sources by the sha gate, but both scripts hard-code the pipeline/census_irfs paths, so pointing them at the public copies is a code edit rather than a command-line option.

docs.title: Placement in one line
docs.text: A model-conditional reading of a scenario path: the tool solves for the sequence of a chosen MMB model's own structural shocks that reproduces the displayed path over twelve quarters, draws the contributions in the panel's units with an explicit residual, and gates every interpretive step — the naming budget, the collinearity flag, the class-view licence — on what the same-model recovery benches actually validated. It is the structural-interpretation counterpart to the accounting satellites: where the fiscal and external blocks derive stocks from the BVAR path by identity, this one reads that path through a model's lens, and it claims no more than the lens.

docs.title: Key references
docs.text: Smets & Wouters, Shocks and Frictions in US Business Cycles (2007, the licensed lens and its class map) · Christiano, Motto & Rostagno, Risk Shocks (2014, the financial-block lens) · Wieland et al., A New Comparative Approach to Macroeconomic Modeling and Policy Analysis (the Macroeconomic Model Base, source of every response file here) · Brayton, Laubach & Reifschneider, The FRB/US Model (the two 54-shock census lenses) · Coenen et al., New Area-Wide Model II (the filter-the-path exercise this decomposition implements) · Christiano, Eichenbaum & Evans, Nominal Rigidities and the Dynamic Effects of a Shock to Monetary Policy (the historical-decomposition reading of stacked impulse responses) · in-repo: pipeline/bench_simple_decomp.m and pipeline/bench_class_recovery.m, with transcripts in docs/paper/simple_decomp_results.txt and docs/paper/class_recovery_results.txt.

docs.title: Euro-area cross-border spillover & harmonization
docs.text:
This page explains how the tool links the euro-area aggregate (EA) and its individual members (DE, FR, IT, ES, …) so that a scenario built on one bloc reaches the others in an economically consistent way — and how the shared building blocks of a monetary union (the ECB policy rate, the risk-free curve, sovereign spreads) are kept coherent across all of them.

If you just want the "how do I use it" version, jump to Using it, step by step.

docs.title: The setup: why members need special treatment
docs.text:
Each member (DE, FR, IT, …) is estimated as its own standalone BVAR (Bayesian VAR). The EA aggregate is a full bloc of the coupled GVAR (Global VAR) (it trades and co-moves with the US, China, etc.). The members are not in the GVAR coupling — they hang off the EA.

That design is deliberate (a member's domestic detail — its fiscal block, its house prices, its sovereign spread — lives in the member model, while cross-border transmission is carried by the aggregate). But it creates three gaps that this feature set closes:

  1. A US or EA scenario you build would never reach a member, because the member isn't in the coupled solve.
  2. The ECB policy rate — one common instrument — was being forecast separately by each member model, so it came out different across members.
  3. There was no direct handle on the euro-area risk-free curve or a country's sovereign spread in the member view.

docs.title: 1. Cross-border spillover: a US/EA scenario reaches the members
docs.text:
When you condition the US or the EA aggregate and press ▶ Solve full GVAR, the tool solves the complete coupled system (including the EA bloc's response). It then reads the EA aggregate's solved deviation and maps it onto each member's foreign/rest-of-area inputs, so the member's own model transmits the area-wide shock into its domestic GDP, inflation, and rates.

  • The member you are viewing shows a small amber note — "Cross-border spillover from the US/EA scenario not yet computed" — with a ▶ Solve full GVAR button, until you run the solve. This is deliberate: the full coupled solve takes a few seconds, so it runs only when you ask for it (pressing the button, or Compute), never automatically on every click.
  • The transmission uses the deviation of the EA path from the member's own baseline (not the raw EA level), so it never injects the gap between the EA and the member's baseline — at a zero scenario it is an exact no-op.

docs.title: 2. The ECB policy rate is common across EA and members
docs.text:
The problem. The euro area has one policy rate, set by the ECB. But because every member was a separate BVAR forecasting its own POLRATE column, the common rate came out different across members — and sometimes implausibly so:

bloc old terminal ECB-rate forecast EA 2.25% DE 0.71% FR 2.55% IT 3.02%

(This was not the long-run "consensus drift" target — the policy rate has no long-run anchor in any bloc. It was purely the separate-model artefact.)

The fix. Every member's policy rate is now pinned to the EA aggregate's POLRATE_EA path — the single common ECB rate — in both the baseline and every scenario. Concretely, POLRATE_<member> is treated as exogenous and driven by the EA rate; the member's own model then re-solves its domestic block in response to the common rate. So:

  • The policy-rate chart is identical across EA and all members.
  • Each member's domestic GDP/inflation baseline responds to the common rate — e.g. Germany, whose rate rises from the old 0.7% to the ~2.25% area path, now shows the correspondingly tighter activity; Italy (rate falling 3.0→2.25%) the opposite.
  • Scenario deviations are unchanged where you don't touch the rate: because the same common-rate pin sits under both the baseline and the scenario, it cancels in (scenario − baseline). Only the level baseline shifts.

One consequence worth knowing

Because the ECB rate is now exogenous and common, conditioning a member variable that would otherwise induce an endogenous domestic rate response (e.g. a large GDP shock) leaves the policy rate on the common path rather than letting the member's own rate drift. That is the correct behaviour for a single area-wide policy rate — the ECB does not set a Germany-specific rate.

docs.title: 3. Conditioning the ECB rate on a member = an area-wide shock
docs.text:
The ECB Policy Rate now appears as a draggable chart in the member's first row. Because it is the common rate, conditioning it on any euro bloc is an area-wide monetary shock:

  • Drag the ECB-rate path on, say, Germany, then press ▶ Solve full GVAR.
  • Your pin is mirrored onto the EA aggregate's POLRATE_EA, the coupled system re-solves, and the new rate propagates to the EA aggregate and every other member.
  • It is one shared rate — editing it on DE then FR edits the same underlying ECB path (last edit wins).

docs.title: 4. The euro risk-free curve (Bund) and the country spread
docs.text:
Members carry their long rate as Bund + spread: a common risk-free benchmark (the German 10-year, YIELD10_DE) plus a country-specific sovereign spread (SPREAD_<member>). Both are now surfaced as draggable charts:

  • EA Long Yield (Bund). Conditioning the benchmark is a common risk-free curve shock: it maps one-for-one onto the area long yield and propagates to every member's risk-free reference.
  • Sovereign Spread (vs Bund). Conditioning a member's spread is a country-specific stress, and it is contagious: it feeds the euro-area long yield in proportion to that country's share of euro-area GDP. Formally, Δ YIELD10_EA = w_member · Δ spread_member, which is exactly the mechanical identity for a GDP-weighted area yield (YIELD10_EA ≈ Bund + Σᵢ wᵢ · spreadᵢ). So a widening Italian spread (weight ≈ 14%) transmits far more to the area than an Estonian one (≈ 0.3%).

The GDP weights are real Eurostat data (current-price GDP, 4-quarter-trailing share of the 20-member euro area (EA20), app/public/data/bvar/gvar/ea_gdp_weights.json) — not assumed. If both a Bund pin and a spread pin are set, their effects add on the area yield.

docs.title: Using it, step by step
docs.text:
1. Build the scenario where it's natural.
    • Area-wide monetary or curve shock → condition ECB Policy Rate or EA Long Yield (Bund) on any euro bloc.
    • Country-specific sovereign stress → condition Sovereign Spread (vs Bund) on that member.
    • A global/US shock → condition the US or EA aggregate.
  2. Press ▶ Solve full GVAR (or Compute). The coupled system solves and the shock propagates to the EA aggregate and every member. On a member, the amber prompt tells you when a solve is pending.
  3. Switch blocs to read the transmission. View the EA aggregate and the other members to see the propagated paths; the policy-rate chart will read the same everywhere.

docs.title: Honest caveats
docs.text:
• The common rate is identical to within a sub-basis-point (~0.005 pp) numerical residual — the in-browser smoother differs infinitesimally from the stored baseline. It is invisible on the charts; a two-decimal tooltip can very occasionally show e.g. 2.24 vs 2.25.
  • Spread contagion is a modelling choice, not an estimated equation: a country's spread feeds the area yield by its GDP weight. It is a transparent, data-grounded pass-through, deliberately simple.
  • Germany is the risk-free anchor: its YIELD10_DE is the Bund, so DE carries a Bund chart but no sovereign-spread chart (its spread is zero by construction).
  • Everything here is forecast conditioning (the Durbin–Koopman smoother), layered on top of the frozen estimated models — no re-estimation is involved.

Implementation: app/src/components/charts/ChartGrid.tsx (the member→EA pin mirror, the rate-driven baseline, the Bund/spread channels), app/src/lib/compute/eaMemberSpillover.ts and useEaMemberSpillover.ts (the EA→member mapping), app/public/data/bvar/gvar/ea_gdp_weights.json (the GDP weights). See also the Fiscal Block and External Block methodology pages.

docs.title: External Block — the balance-of-payments satellite (Trade Balance + Current Account + NFA/GDP)
docs.text:
The external block estimates the external drivers inside the BVAR (trade flows and the exchange rate) and derives the reporting variables — trade balance, current account, and the net international investment position (net foreign assets, NFA) as a share of GDP — by accounting identity. This is the exact same division of labour as the fiscal block: a reduced-form model is never allowed to freely forecast a stock (there, public debt; here, NFA). Instead the BVAR forecasts the flows and the FX index, and a separate, side-effect-free accounting module rolls the stock forward by the balance-of-payments identity, seeded from a real, sourced anchor.

Together the fiscal block, this external block, and the monetary core complete the IMF FPP monetary–fiscal–external triad of sectoral consistency: fiscal rolls the debt stock from a budget identity, external rolls the NFA stock from the BoP identity, and both share the same two-layer pattern (BVAR flow generator + identity recursion) and the same %-of-GDP annual-ratio convention.

docs.title: The shared backbone (identical to the fiscal block)
docs.text:
Both satellites separate "forecast the macro + sector flows in the BVAR" from "derive the sector stock by accounting." Neither lets the reduced form forecast the stock directly.

  • Fiscal: BVAR forecasts revenue/GDP, primary-expenditure/GDP, the effective rate and the SFA → app/src/lib/compute/fiscalAccounting.ts rolls debt/GDP forward by the FPP/DSA debt-dynamics identity, seeded by d0 in fiscal_meta.json.
  • External: BVAR forecasts exports, imports, GDP and the FX index → app/src/lib/compute/externalAccounting.ts rolls NFA/GDP forward by the BoP identity, seeded by nfa0 (real net-IIP / nominal GDP) in external_meta.json.

The authoritative implementation is computeExternalBlock in app/src/lib/compute/externalAccounting.ts. It is read-only and side-effect-free: it consumes a level-space forecast path and returns per-quarter arrays of length H. It is wired into app/src/components/charts/ChartGrid.tsx exactly the way the fiscal block is — a derived useMemo, a per-draw band loop, and synthetic chart traces — and is fully gated on the presence of a chartable external_meta.json (a bloc without one renders nothing, with zero band work).

docs.title: Element-by-element mapping
docs.text:
Concept IMF BoP / FPP external sector This tool Exports / imports (drivers) goods+services trade flows estimated BVAR level vars (US XH/MH; EA EXP_EA/IMP_EA) GDP (denominator) nominal GDP estimated BVAR level var (GDPH / GDP_EA) Exchange rate (driver) NEER / REER estimated BVAR log var (US FXTWM; EA NEER_EA) Trade balance exports − imports, % GDP derived TB = 100·(X−M)/gdp$ Primary income on NFA investment income on the net IIP derived income = iNFA·NFA₋₁/100 (imputed return) Current account trade balance + primary income (+ transfers) derived CA = TB + income FX valuation effect revaluation of FX-denominated net assets derived val = −fxShare·NFA₋₁·ΔFX NFA / net IIP path NFAₜ = NFA₋₁/(1+gₜ) + CAₜ/4 + valuationₜ derived ratio recursion (BoP identity + GDP-growth dilution) NFA seed observed net IIP / GDP sourced nfa0 in external_meta.json (real, per bloc)

The NFA recursion is the BoP stock-flow identity in percent-of-GDP form — the inherited ratio is diluted by nominal GDP growth (/(1+g)), then the net international investment position changes by the current-account flow plus valuation (revaluation) effects, the same decomposition the IMF/ECB external statistics and the Lane–Milesi-Ferretti External Wealth of Nations dataset use.

docs.title: The recursion, precisely
docs.text:
Read the units block at the top of externalAccounting.ts before editing anything here. Per forecast quarter t = 0 … H−1, read off the level-space forecast path (100·log for log vars; level for lin):

  • exports / imports / GDP — log vars; the quantity is exp(level/100). Trade balance is a % of GDP, so the numerator (exports − imports) and the denominator gdp$ must be in a common nominal scale. For US (XH/MH/GDPH all real chained Bil USD) and EA (EXP_EA/IMP_EA/GDP_EA all real, common units) they are, so the ratio is real-trade-balance / real-GDP and validates against the published BoP figure.
  • the FX index (idx.fx, log var: US FXTWM, EA NEER_EA, CN REER_CN) — "up = home currency appreciates." A rise lowers the domestic-currency value of FX-denominated net assets, hence the negative valuation sign below.
  • iNFA (idx-level iNFA, % p.a.) — the imputed return on the NFA stock, a modeling default (~3%), flagged in external_meta.json (_flags).
  • fxShare (fxShare, fraction in [0,1]) — the FX-exposed share of the NFA stock, a modeling default (~0.4), flagged.

The seed nfa0 (initial NFA/GDP, %) is the real, sourced net-IIP/GDP anchor from external_meta.json.

docs.title: Per-quarter recursion (using lagged NFA NFA₋₁ so the loop stays explicit)
docs.text:
With NFA₋₁ = nfa0 at t=0 and NFA₋₁ = nfa[t−1] thereafter, and prev the previous level row (prevLevelRow at t=0, for the FX diff seam):

  1. Trade balance (% of GDP, annual ratio): TBₜ = 100·(exp(levelₜ[exports]/100) − exp(levelₜ[imports]/100)) / exp(levelₜ[gdp]/100) (externalAccounting.ts:104).
  2. Primary income on the NFA stock: incomeₜ = iNFA · NFA₋₁ / 100 (externalAccounting.ts:106). This is the imputed-return channel (modeling default), the only place iNFA enters.
  3. Current account (% of GDP, annual): CAₜ = TBₜ + incomeₜ (externalAccounting.ts:107).
  4. FX valuation effect this quarter: with dFXₜ = levelₜ[fx] − prev[fx] (Δ of 100·log FX), valₜ = −fxShare · NFA₋₁ · dFXₜ / 100 (externalAccounting.ts:109–110). A home appreciation (dFX>0) cuts the home value of FX-denominated net assets, so for a net creditor it reduces NFA and for a net debtor (nfa0<0) it raises NFA (FX-denominated net liabilities shrink).
  5. Roll the stock forward (the ratio-form BoP identity), quarterly: NFAₜ = NFA₋₁/(1+gₜ) + CAₜ/4 + valₜ (externalAccounting.ts), where gₜ is quarterly nominal GDP growth (decimal, the same construction as the fiscal block) — the division is the automatic denominator effect on a %-of-GDP stock. The current account is an annual ratio so it enters as a quarter-share (/4); the valuation effect is already this quarter's. The return on the stock enters through the income leg of CAₜ, computed on the undiluted NFA₋₁ (the dropped cross-terms are second-order).
  6. Derived reporting variable: Δ(NFA/GDP)ₜ = NFAₜ − NFA₋₁ (externalAccounting.ts:119).

The recursion returns { tb, income, ca, valuation, nfa, dNfa }, all length H.

docs.title: Anchors and which blocs have an external block
docs.text:
The seed nfa0 is never invented; it is a real, sourced net-IIP/GDP figure (per the absolute no-synthetic rule). A bloc whose IIP cannot be verified, or whose trade flows and GDP are not in a common scale, ships without a chartable external_meta.json and renders no external charts.

Bloc External block? nfa0 (% GDP) Source TB anchor (h0) US Yes (renders) −66.75 FRED IIPUSNETIQ (US Net IIP, −21,270,237 Mil USD, 2026-01-01) / FRED GDP (nominal SAAR, 31,865.721 Bil USD, 2026Q1). US = large net debtor. −3.80% (deficit; published −3 to −4% range) EA Yes (renders) +11.0 ECB official release "Euro area quarterly balance of payments and international investment position: Q4 2025" — net assets EUR 1.76 tn = 11.0% of EA GDP. EA ≈ small net creditor. +3.59% (modest surplus, net exporter) CN Yes (renders, via unit reconciliation) +20.35 SAFE "China's IIP at end-2025" — net external assets USD 4,071.3 bn; NBS 2025 nominal GDP CNY 140.1879 tn = USD 20.01 tn (implied CNY/USD 7.006) ⇒ +20.35% GDP. Cross-check BoFiT ~20%. CN = net creditor. +4.46% (goods-trade surplus; published ~4–5% range) JP, UK, CA No (no external_meta.json) — IIP not yet verified for these blocs (flagged) —

So US, EA and CN are the blocs that render the external block. CN required a units reconciliation (see caveat 5) because its trade flows and GDP are in incompatible native units; with the real, sourced conversion factors it now ships externalChartable:true. JP / UK / CA ship no external_meta.json at all (loader's Promise.allSettled resolves 404 → null → nothing renders, no band work).

The iNFA (~3% p.a.) and fxShare (~0.4) parameters are modeling defaults shipped clearly flagged (the _flags key in each external_meta.json), exactly like the structural-constant SFA in the fiscal block — they are not estimated or sourced.

docs.title: Honest caveats (read before relying on the output)
docs.text: These are documented honestly because the tool is a live research instrument.

docs.title: 1. The trade balance is a real-VOLUME balance, not the nominal customs CA (US, EA)
docs.text: For US and EA the trade flows and GDP are in a common real scale (US real chained Bil USD; EA real, common units), so the ratio is a real-trade-volume / real-GDP balance. It validates against the published nominal BoP trade balance to within a relative-price wedge (US ≈ −3.8%, EA ≈ +3.5%), but it is not the nominal customs/BoP current account to the decimal. Terms-of-trade swings between export and import prices are not captured because the BVAR carries real volumes, not separate export/import deflators. Treat the levels as economically faithful, the high-frequency wiggles as volume-driven.

docs.title: 2. Primary income is IMPUTED, not estimated (iNFA)
docs.text: The primary-income leg of the current account is income = iNFA·NFA₋₁/100 with a modeling-default imputed return iNFA ≈ 3% p.a. — it is not an estimated BVAR variable and not sourced. It is flagged in external_meta.json (_flags), like the structural SFA. Because income compounds on the lagged NFA stock, a more-negative NFA path mechanically produces a more-negative income drag (and vice versa); this is a deliberate, transparent channel, but it is a parameterized assumption, not data.

docs.title: 3. FX valuation uses an external parameter (fxShare)
docs.text: The valuation (revaluation) effect val = −fxShare·NFA₋₁·ΔFX uses a modeling-default FX-exposed share fxShare ≈ 0.4 — the fraction of the net IIP denominated in foreign currency. It is not sourced and is flagged like iNFA. The sign convention (home appreciation cuts the home value of FX net assets) means a fiscal expansion that appreciates the currency can, for a net debtor (nfa0<0, e.g. US), produce a positive valuation gain (FX-denominated net liabilities shrink) — an economically correct J-curve/valuation channel, kept ON in the live charts. The unconfounded twin-deficit signal is therefore read off the trade/CA flow in the medium-term window, not the long-horizon NFA stock, whose dynamics are valuation-rich.

docs.title: 4. nfa0 is the EXTERNAL seed — real, sourced, per bloc
docs.text: The NFA recursion is only as anchored as its seed. nfa0 is a real net-IIP/GDP figure sourced per bloc (US: FRED IIPUSNETIQ/GDP; EA: ECB Q4-2025 IIP release; CN: SAFE end-2025 IIP). It is never invented. If a bloc's IIP cannot be verified it ships without an external block (JP/UK/CA today). After any re-estimation that changes a bloc's variable order, re-verify the positional idx in external_meta.json (exports/imports/gdp/deflator/fx) — the indices are positional and not auto-regenerated, the same staleness hazard the fiscal block flags.

docs.title: 5. CN units reconciliation — incompatible native units brought to a common nominal-USD ratio
docs.text:
CN is the one bloc whose trade flows and GDP are not in a common native scale, so the raw level paths cannot be ratioed directly (the un-converted TB/GDP is off by ~10⁵). The mismatch is purely one of units and frequency, not of missing data, so it is resolved by a small set of real, sourced conversion factors (units.* in external_meta.json) — no FX rate or flow is fabricated.

Updated (surgical CN-only real-GDP re-estimate, 2026-06). GDP_CN is now a real chain-linked volume index (not nominal CNY), so the GDP denominator is reconstructed in nominal USD via the gdpKind:'realIndexDeflate' branch: gdp$ = exp(gdp/100)·exp(deflator/100)·usdBase, with a single calibrated usdBase = 158760958.8679 scalar (CN's external block carries tradeFreqMult: 3 and gdpKind:'realIndexDeflate'). This pins the CN goods-trade balance to the published +4.46% of GDP at the historical anchor. The legacy nominal-CNY path below (gdpScale/fxToUsd) is retained for historical reference only and is no longer the active conversion for CN. This was a CN-only graft; the other 32 GVAR blocs are byte-identical to the prior working model.

The legacy native units, verified from the last historical level row (exp(level/100)):

Series Native unit exp(level/100) (last row) Conversion GDP_CN (legacy nominal) nominal CNY, millions, quarterly 35,984,541 (≈ 36 tn CNY/quarter) gdpScale=1e6 (millions → ones), then ÷ fxToUsd (CNY → USD) EXP_CN nominal USD, monthly-average flow 314,673,049,926 (≈ $315 bn/month) × tradeFreqMult=3 (monthly → quarterly) IMP_CN nominal USD, monthly-average flow 239,543,292,627 (≈ $240 bn/month) × tradeFreqMult=3 (monthly → quarterly)

The factors:

  • usdBase = 158760958.8679 (active) — realIndexDeflate scalar that maps the real chain-linked exp(gdp/100)·exp(deflator/100) product into nominal USD, calibrated so the CN trade balance lands at the published +4.46% of GDP at the anchor.
  • gdpScale = 1e6 (legacy nominal path) — when GDP_CN was in millions of CNY; multiplying exp(gdp/100) by 1e6 put the denominator in ones (CNY), matching the trade flows in ones (USD).
  • fxToUsd = 6.7686 (legacy nominal path) — the real CNY/USD spot rate; GDP-in-CNY ÷ this = GDP-in-USD. Sourced from FRED series DEXCHUS, latest non-missing observation 2026-06-18. Cross-confirmed against its primary upstream source — the Federal Reserve H.10 Foreign Exchange Rates release (federalreserve.gov/releases/h10/current, release dated 2026-06-22, China spot for 2026-06-18), a byte-exact match. Not synthetic.
  • tradeFreqMult = 3 — EXP_CN/IMP_CN are monthly-average USD flows while GDP is quarterly; ×3 quarterizes the flows so numerator and denominator share a frequency.

Applied to the recursion (externalAccounting.ts):

gdp$  = exp(gdp/100) · gdpScale / fxToUsd          // CNY-millions → USD
exp$  = exp(exports/100) · tradeFreqMult           // monthly-USD → quarterly-USD
imp$  = exp(imports/100) · tradeFreqMult
TB    = 100 · (exp$ − imp$) / gdp$                 // % of GDP, common nominal-USD ratio

which gives, at the forecast anchor, TB ≈ +4.46% of GDP — squarely in China's published goods-trade surplus range (~4–5% of GDP). CN therefore now ships externalChartable:true and renders the external block on this common-USD ratio.

These factors are pure unit/frequency conversions, not data. Each native series keeps its own real sourced value; the factors only restate them in a single nominal-USD, quarterly scale. The default for any bloc that ships no units.* (US, EA) is gdpScale=fxToUsd=tradeFreqMult=1, so the US/EA paths are byte-identical to before this change (guarded by the byte-identity test). The CN factors are load-bearing — a test asserts that without them the ratio is absurd (>10³) — so a future editor must never drop them back to the raw level paths. The CN units behaviour is pinned by app/src/__tests__/compute/externalAccounting.test.ts.

docs.title: 6. The displayed NFA path is a PASSIVE accounting recursion (no debt/NFA feedback)
docs.text: Like the fiscal block's deployed computeFiscalBlock, the external recursion has no endogenous feedback from the NFA stock back onto the BVAR drivers (no NFA→FX risk premium, no NFA→trade adjustment). The trade flows and FX are debt-agnostic BVAR baselines; the income and valuation legs layer on the lagged stock with no double-counting. This is a transparent passive recursion, not a sustainability model — a possible future extension.

docs.title: Bands
docs.text: The external bands (TB / CA / NFA at q16/q84) are a faithful clone of the fiscal default-mode band: they are computed per-draw via computeExternalBlock on the unconditional level path, parallel-shifted by (scenarioMean − baselineMean), and injected into the three chart traces. They are cleared everywhere the fiscal bands are. The synthetic chart bvarIdx is 9100+si (distinct from the fiscal 9000+) with draggable:null, so the j-indexed conditioning / band / forecast loops skip it — the external path is strictly additive and the δc=0 + external no-op stays byte-exact with the fiscal no-op.

docs.title: Placement in one line
docs.text: A compact, interactive realization of the IMF FPP external sector: the BVAR forecasts the trade flows and the exchange rate, and a passive balance-of-payments stock-flow recursion rolls NFA/GDP forward from a real, sourced net-IIP seed (trade balance + imputed primary income + FX valuation). It is the external leg of the monetary–fiscal–external triad, built on the identical two-layer pattern as the fiscal block, shipped for US, EA and CN (CN via a real, sourced nominal-USD units reconciliation; JP/UK/CA pending verified IIP).

docs.title: Key references
docs.text: IMF, Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual (BPM6, the CA/IIP identity and valuation decomposition) · IMF Financial Programming (FPP, four-sector consistency) · ECB, Euro area balance of payments and international investment position (quarterly statistical releases) · Lane & Milesi-Ferretti, The External Wealth of Nations (net-IIP construction, valuation effects) · Obstfeld & Rogoff, Foundations of International Macroeconomics (the intertemporal current account and NFA accumulation) · Gourinchas & Rey, International Financial Adjustment (valuation channel of external adjustment).

docs.title: Fiscal Block — relation to the CBO and IMF FPP frameworks
docs.text: The fiscal block estimates the fiscal drivers inside the BVAR and derives the reporting variables (deficit, debt service, debt-to-GDP, gross financing needs) by accounting identity. This is the same division of labour used by the U.S. Congressional Budget Office (CBO) and by IMF Financial Programming and Policies (FPP) / debt sustainability — not a coincidence; the design is built on their shared backbone.

docs.title: The shared backbone
docs.text:
Both frameworks separate "forecast the macro + fiscal flows" from "derive debt and the balances by accounting." Neither lets a reduced-form model freely forecast the debt stock.

  • CBO runs a conditional BVAR (Minnesota/GLP shrinkage, hierarchical tightness — the same prior family this tool already uses; Conditional Forecasting With a Bayesian VAR, 2023) purely as a macro scenario generator; those paths feed a separate, simplified budget module that produces revenues, outlays, net interest, deficit, and debt. Budget accounting lives outside the BVAR.
  • IMF FPP is the four-sector (real / fiscal / monetary / external) consistency framework. The fiscal block forecasts revenue, expenditure, and financing, then imposes the government budget constraint and debt-dynamics identity to get debt, with a stock-flow-adjustment (SFA) residual closing it. The modern quarterly incarnation is the IMF QMFF (A Novel Quarterly Macroeconomic Forecasting Framework, 2026): a QPM core + FPP sectoral accounting, linkable to the IMF debt tools (DDT / DDT_GFN).

This tool is that division of labour: the BVAR (extended to carry the fiscal flow ratios) is the scenario generator; app/src/lib/compute/fiscalAccounting.ts is the budget/accounting module. We fuse CBO's "macro BVAR" and "budget module" into one interactive tool, with the accounting module implemented as the IMF FPP/DSA debt-dynamics recursion.

docs.title: Element-by-element mapping
docs.text:
Concept CBO IMF FPP / DSA This tool Macro determinants (g, π, rates) macro model + conditional BVAR real + monetary sectors existing BVAR vars (GDPH, JGDP, 2Y, +new 10Y) Revenue revenue module, elasticities to wages/profits/GDP revenue (% GDP) estimated BVAR flow revenue/GDP Primary spending mandatory + discretionary outlays primary expenditure (% GDP) estimated BVAR flow primexp/GDP Effective interest rate weighted-avg rate on outstanding debt (lags market) effective rate on debt estimated BVAR var EFFI Net interest / debt service eff. rate × debt held by public i_eff · d₋₁ derived int = i_eff·d₋₁ Primary balance deficit excl. net interest rev − non-interest exp derived pb = rev − primexp Overall deficit outlays − revenues −(pb − int) derived deficit = int − pb Debt path Debtₜ = Debt₋₁ + deficit + other means of financing dₜ = d₋₁(1+i)/(1+gⁿ) − pb + sfa derived recursion (the FPP/DSA equation) Snowball / (i−g) interest-vs-growth in long-run outlook Fiscal Monitor decomposition derived snowball decomposition Gross financing needs issuance to fund operations primary deficit + interest + amortization derived gfn SFA / "other means of financing" OMF line stock-flow adjustment the sfa soft-identity closure Conditioning on official/policy paths current-law & alternative scenarios WEO-consistent soft conditions the tool's scenario conditioning (drag driver paths)

The debt recursion is the IMF DSA / DDT–DDT_GFN equation — same (1+i)/(1+gⁿ) snowball, same SFA term, same primary-vs-overall-balance distinction and sign convention (primary balance positive = surplus). Both frameworks require debt service to use the effective average rate on the stock, not the policy/market rate — hence we estimate EFFI rather than reusing the 2Y.

docs.title: The debt recursion, precisely
docs.text:
This section pins the exact arithmetic the accounting module runs, so the manual and the code never drift. The authoritative implementation is app/src/lib/compute/fiscalAccounting.ts, which exposes two recursions:

  • computeFiscalBlock (fiscalAccounting.ts:158) — the live forecast/band path (called per draw from runGvarBandSolve.ts). It reads the drivers off the level-space path and rolls the debt identity forward. It does not apply the Bohn / risk-premium feedback (pb = revenue − primexp exactly; no γ/β term).
  • runFiscalRecursion (fiscalAccounting.ts:66) — the array-level core that adds the optional active debt-feedback levers (the Bohn fiscal-reaction-function γ and the risk-premium β).

⚠️ runFiscalRecursion has NO live UI/production caller. As of this writing it is invoked only from the test suite (__tests__/compute/fiscalAccounting.test.ts, __tests__/compute/fiscal-backcast.test.ts) — the γ/β-lever path is test-covered only, not wired into the production forecast flow (the band/forecast path goes exclusively through computeFiscalBlock). The feedback levers are documented and validated but currently dormant.

The roll-forward identity below is identical in both; the feedback terms (step 1's γ, step 2's β) apply only in runFiscalRecursion. Read the units block at the top of the file (fiscalAccounting.ts:7) before editing anything here.

docs.title: Inputs (the BVAR-estimated drivers)
docs.text:
Per forecast quarter t = 0 … H−1, read off the level-space forecast path:

  • revenue / GDP and primary expenditure / GDP — % of GDP, expressed as an annual ratio (the 4-quarter-sum over 4-quarter-nominal-GDP ratio the BVAR carries as a lin variable).
  • the effective rate EFFI (idx.effRate, % p.a., the average rate on the outstanding stock): the deployed form for all six fiscal blocs (US, EA, JP, UK, CA, CN), where interest = EFFI · d₋₁ / 100. The recursion also supports an estimated debt-service / GDP column (idx.debtService, % of GDP) — when present that is the endogenous interest and the effective rate is backed out of it — but idx.debtService is not in the deployed fiscal_meta.json of any bloc, so the live path takes the effective-rate branch.
  • stock-flow adjustment SFA (idx.sfa, % of GDP annual ratio) — read per-quarter off the level path when an SFA column is estimated, so the debt projection carries the deficit–debt discrepancy forward with its own dynamics and bands; otherwise a constant sfaDefault (or zeros).
  • nominal GDP growth gⁿ — built from the level path as gNomQ = Δ(real-GDP 100·log) + Δ(deflator 100·log) (% per quarter), i.e. ((levelPaths[t][idx.gdp] − prev[idx.gdp]) + (levelPaths[t][idx.deflator] − prev[idx.deflator]))/100 (fiscalAccounting.ts:169). The growth and rate are quarterized internally while the flow reporting variables stay annual.

The seed d₀ (initial debt/GDP, %) and the feedback anchor d* (default d₀) come from fiscal_meta.json (d0).

docs.title: Per-quarter recursion (using lagged debt d₋₁ so the loop stays explicit)
docs.text:
With dₚᵣₑᵥ = d₀ at t=0 and dₚᵣₑᵥ = debt[t−1] thereafter (fiscalAccounting.ts:170):

  1. Primary balance pb_t = rev_t − primexp_t (live path, fiscalAccounting.ts:171), plus the optional Bohn fiscal-reaction-function + γ·(d₋₁ − d*) in runFiscalRecursion (fiscalAccounting.ts:98; γ default 0.03 ⇒ consolidation as debt rises above d*).
  2. Interest / debt service (% of GDP): int_t = EFFI_t · d₋₁ / 100 (deployed effective-rate branch, fiscalAccounting.ts:177), or int_t = dsvc_t directly when a debt-service column is estimated; runFiscalRecursion additionally adds the debt-level risk premium β·max(0, d₋₁ − d*)·d₋₁/100 (fiscalAccounting.ts:94–95, β default 0). The effective rate is backed out for the roll-forward and for display: i_eff_t = int_t · 100 / d₋₁ (fiscalAccounting.ts:178, 96).
  3. Roll the stock forward (the IMF DSA / FPP debt-dynamics identity), quarterly: d_t = d₋₁ · (1 + i_eff_t/400) / (1 + gⁿ_t/100) − pb_t/4 + sfa_t/4  (fiscalAccounting.ts:185). Here i_eff_t/400 is the quarterized effective rate (so d₋₁·(1+iQ) = d₋₁ + int_t/4), the /(1+gⁿ/100) term is the denominator that shrinks the ratio when nominal GDP grows, and the primary balance and SFA enter as quarter-shares (/4, since they are annual ratios).
  4. Derived reporting variables, all falling straight out of the same identity:
  5. overall deficit deficit_t = int_t − pb_t (fiscalAccounting.ts:188);
  6. implied change in the ratio Δ(debt/GDP)_t = d_t − d₋₁ (fiscalAccounting.ts:186, the chart's third-row derived variable);
  7. the snowball (automatic debt dynamics) snowball_t = [(1+iQ)/(1+gQ) − 1]·d₋₁ — the interest-minus-growth (i−g) contribution the IMF Fiscal Monitor decomposition isolates (fiscalAccounting.ts:190);
  8. gross financing needs gfn_t = deficit_t + amortization_t (fiscalAccounting.ts:191).

docs.title: SFA closure and the inverse map
docs.text:
The SFA is the soft-identity residual that closes the deficit-vs-debt gap. It is estimated as its own BVAR column (the idx.sfa path) and forecast with its own dynamics and bands; the deployed debt roll-forward, however, uses the structural constant sfaDefault (the long-run SFA mean), not the per-quarter forecast SFA column (computeFiscalBlock lines 192–200). The forecast column is dragged to spurious extremes by the δc long-run/consensus anchors' cross-response (e.g. UK −3.2→−8.2), which would collapse the projected debt path; the structural constant is the economically-correct long-run residual. The recursion is also invertible: requiredPrimaryBalance (fiscalAccounting.ts:217) solves the same equation for the primary balance that pins debt to a target path, pb_t = 4·[(d₋₁ + int_t/4)/(1 + gⁿ_t/100) − d_target,t] + sfa_t, which the tool feeds back as a conditioning constraint (revenue − primexp). Because effective rate and growth respond to the primary balance through the BVAR, the caller iterates invert → condition → re-read i,g → re-invert (1–2 passes converge).

The exact quarterly convention here is pinned by the historical back-cast test (reconstructed debt/GDP vs observed; fixture app/src/__tests__/fixtures/us_fiscal_backcast.json) — the identity error is ≈ 0 except for the modelled SFA, exactly the consistency check both CBO and FPP demand.

docs.title: Even-coupon EFFI for coupon-lumpy blocs
docs.text:
For most economies interest is paid smoothly enough that the quarterly EFFI is well-behaved. Eight of the wider (RoW) fiscal blocs, however, pay interest on an annual/semiannual coupon calendar — one or two quarters carry the whole year's coupon and the others carry near-zero. Fed raw into EFFI = 400·interest_t / debt_{t-1}, that lumpiness makes EFFI a near-Nyquist sawtooth and drives a companion root toward −1, which then contaminates the SFA residual and (through the BVAR) neighbouring series. This was the diagnosed root cause of the EFFI/SFA jaggedness in those blocs.

The fix (verified pipeline/build_fiscal22_columns.py:58–100,178–181) is to distribute the coupon evenly across the year before estimation for the flagged blocs:

EVEN_INTEREST = {CL, CO, CR, ID, IL, MX, TR, ZA}

These were detected by a systematic within-year pattern — calendar-R² > 0.5 and CV > 0.25 on the raw interest flows, or near-perfect quarterly alternation. even_distribute_years() replaces, within each COMPLETE calendar year, the four quarterly interest payments by their mean (the annual total is preserved exactly); the trailing partial year uses the trailing-four-quarter mean. Two consequences define the treatment:

  • EFFI becomes the accrual borrowing cost. EFFI = 400·evened_interest_t / debt_{t-1} now measures the accrued cost of carrying the stock, not the calendar timing of the cash coupon.
  • Primary expenditure keeps the RAW interest (te − intr = true non-interest spending), and the exact debt-identity residual SFA absorbs the genuine cash-vs-accrual timing. The evening moves the timing wedge out of EFFI and into SFA, which is precisely why these eight blocs also carry seasonal dummies in estimation (so the residual's within-year cycle is a bounded deterministic term rather than a spurious explosive root; see the seasonal-dummy treatment in REESTIMATING_MODELS.md §1.3).

Because only the distribution of a preserved annual total changes, the debt-dynamics identity still closes exactly (closure error ~1e-14, same one-step back-cast gate as the six advanced blocs). The sawtooth is removed — mean absolute quarterly EFFI change falls sharply (e.g. CL 4.82→0.11, MX 4.95→0.21, ZA 5.00→0.25) — and the offending near-Nyquist companion root moves off −1 (ZA −0.973→−0.634, MX −0.953→−0.659, CL −0.965→−0.588). The operational rebuild step (the --force re-append) is in REESTIMATING_MODELS.md §2.3.

docs.title: Where we follow faithfully
docs.text:
• The two-layer separation (BVAR/flows + identity recursion) — the core of both frameworks.
  • Conditional forecasting itself: the tool's existing scenario engine (condition on a few driver paths → consistent forecast of the rest) is CBO's conditional-BVAR method and FPP's "official paths as soft information." The fiscal block just adds the accounting layer on top.
  • SFA soft-identity closure, primary/overall balance definitions, effective-rate debt service.

docs.title: Where we extend beyond the simplified versions
docs.text:
• Endogenous, jointly-estimated fiscal flows. CBO's budget module is largely elasticity-based; we let the BVAR's reduced form capture revenue/expenditure cyclicality jointly with the macro block — closer to the ECB mixed-frequency fiscal BVAR and the IMF QMFF than to CBO's simplest module.
  • Debt-feedback channels (documented; DORMANT — not in the live path) — a risk-premium channel i_eff += β·(d₋₁−d*) and a Bohn fiscal-reaction-function pb += γ·(d₋₁−d*) (γ≈0.03 default) are implemented only in runFiscalRecursion, which has zero production callers (test-suite only, see the ⚠️ note above). The deployed computeFiscalBlock path — the one wired to every displayed debt chart and band — runs with β=γ=0 and there is no UI control for them. So the live tool has no endogenous debt→primary-balance reaction (Bohn) and no debt→yield risk premium; the debt path is a passive accounting recursion. CBO's simplified debt-service tool likewise does not endogenize macro feedback; FPP/DSA usually handle it via scenarios. These channels are a possible future extension toward IMF SRDSF "snowball realism" and the Bohn / fiscal-fatigue sustainability literature; because debt is not a BVAR variable, î_eff/p̂b are debt-agnostic baselines, so the +β/+γ terms would layer on with no double-counting (and, using lagged debt, the recursion stays explicit) were they ever activated.

docs.title: Where we deliberately simplify
docs.text:
• No line-item decomposition — CBO splits revenue (individual income / payroll / corporate / excise) and outlays (Social Security / Medicare / Medicaid / discretionary). We estimate aggregate general-government revenue and primary expenditure; the BVAR subsumes the elasticities but not the components.
  • Not the full four-sector FPP — only the fiscal block plus its macro linkages through the BVAR's correlations (no monetary-survey or BoP identities). A fiscal-block extension of a macro BVAR, not a complete financial program.
  • SFA is a closure/scenario term, not a modelled valuation/FX/contingent-liability block (Phase 2/3).
  • No amortization/maturity profile for GFN, and no accrual↔cash bridge / mixed-frequency in v1.

docs.title: Known issues and limitations (flagged, not yet fixed)
docs.text: These are documented honestly because the tool is a live research instrument. They are flagged for fix, not resolved — read this section before relying on the affected output.

docs.title: 1. China debt: nominal-GDP inflation double-count (material)
docs.text:
The debt-snowball roll-forward shrinks the debt ratio by nominal GDP growth, built as gNomQ = Δ(real-GDP) + Δ(deflator) in 100·log space (fiscalAccounting.ts:169). For the five advanced fiscal blocs idx.gdp correctly points at a real GDP series, so — unlike China below — the growth term does not double-count prices. The deflator term, however, is a true GDP deflator only for the US (idx.gdp = GDPH, idx.deflator = JGDP, idx 7). The other four advanced blocs deflate with a consumer price index, not a GDP deflator (verified against each bloc's spec.json + fiscal_meta.json): EA GDP_EA real + HICP_EA (idx 6), JP GDP_JP real + CPI_JP (idx 7), UK GDP_UK real + CPI_UK (idx 8), CA GDP_CA real + CPI_CA (idx 8). Because real GDP already strips out prices, adding a CPI (rather than the matching GDP deflator) is a CPI-vs-deflator wedge in the nominal-growth term for EA/JP/UK/CA, not the double-price-counting error CN suffers.

For China this was previously wrong but is now fixed (surgical CN-only re-estimate, 2026-06). The CN model historically shipped a single nominal GDP series (spec.json name "CN Nominal GDP (quarterly)"), so the growth term became gNomQ = Δ(nominal GDP) + Δ(CPI) and added the price level twice — biasing the CN debt-to-GDP path. The CN block has since been re-estimated against real GDP: spec.json var 0 is now "CN Real GDP (quarterly, chain-linked SA volume index, base 2011Q1=100)", CN/fiscal_meta.json sets idx.gdpIsNominal = false, and the growth term is now the correct real-GDP + deflator nominal growth used by the advanced blocs. This was a CN-only graft — the surgical fix re-estimated and replaced only the CN bloc; the other 32 GVAR blocs are byte-identical to the prior working model (the earlier full 33-bloc re-run degraded them and was reverted). The CN debt-to-GDP path is now quantitative on the same footing as US/EA/JP/UK/CA.

docs.title: 2. Positional fiscal indices can go stale (fiscal_meta.json)
docs.text: computeFiscalBlock resolves every driver by integer column index from fiscal_meta.json (idx.gdp / deflator / revenue / primaryExp / effRate / sfa). Those indices are positional, and the MATLAB porters (export_bvar_country.m, export_bvar_gvar*.m, export_bvar_euro_fsap.m) do not regenerate fiscal_meta.json — it is maintained by separate scripts (build_fiscal_*.py, pipeline/fix_fiscal_meta_indices.mjs). So any change to a bloc's variable order silently desynchronizes the fiscal indices, and the recursion then reads the wrong columns. This was the cause of a recent EA/UK debt explosion (fixed in commit a42a2db, "Fix explosive fiscal debt (stale fiscal_meta indices)"). After any re-estimation that touches variable order, regenerate / re-verify fiscal_meta.json for every fiscal bloc before trusting the debt path.

docs.title: 3. Long-run anchor tilt does not filter non-finite draws [OBSOLETE — mechanism removed]
docs.text: The entropic long-run-anchor tilt (formerly app/src/lib/compute/longRunTilt.ts) has been removed and superseded by the deterministic driftSetter.ts display translation — a rigid, band-coherent S_h·δc shift toward the target. The tilt's failure mode described here (a singular / near-unit-root draw returning a NaN steady state that poisoned the soft-max weight sum, emptying the anchor band with no warning) no longer applies: driftSetter.ts does no per-draw reweighting.

docs.title: 4. Conditional band uses the filtered (not smoothed) covariance
docs.text:
The conditional-forecast mean is the Durbin–Koopman smoothed path, but the band variance is read from the filtered covariance filteredP[t] (app/src/lib/compute/kalman.ts:404–407). The filtered covariance at quarter t does not yet incorporate information from a future pin, so for quarters preceding a forward conditioning point the band is overstated (wider than the true smoothed band). This applies to any conditioned fiscal driver pinned at a future date.

For the empirical out-of-sample density caveats (the GVAR predictive intervals are over-confident at short horizons — a separate, opposite issue from the conditioning band above), see the Empirical Evaluation page.

docs.title: Placement in one line
docs.text: A compact, interactive realization of CBO's "conditional-BVAR → budget-accounting" division of labour, with the accounting layer implemented as the IMF FPP/DSA debt-dynamics recursion (snowball + SFA). The displayed debt path is a passive accounting recursion; the active-debt-feedback and Bohn-reaction-function channels are documented and validated but dormant (test-only, no live caller) — a possible future extension. It sits methodologically between CBO's simplified budget module and the IMF's QMFF / DDT debt tools. The Step-1 historical back-cast (reconstructed debt/GDP vs observed, identity error ≈ 0 except modelled SFA) is exactly the consistency check both frameworks demand.

docs.title: Key references
docs.text: CBO, The Budget and Economic Outlook (current-law baseline, budget mechanics) · CBO, Conditional Forecasting With a Bayesian VAR (2023) · IMF, Fiscal Monitor (debt decomposition, snowball) · IMF, A Novel Quarterly Macroeconomic Forecasting Framework (QMFF, 2026) · IMF, DDT / DDT_GFN debt tools · IMF MAC SRDSF (realism, fan charts) · Bohn, The Behavior of U.S. Public Debt and Deficits (fiscal reaction function) · Favero & Giavazzi, Debt and the Effects of Fiscal Policy (debt feedback in fiscal VARs).

docs.title: Fiscal Debt/GDP Trajectory Audit — Big-6 Economies
docs.text:
Date: 2026-06-25 · Branch: feature/trend-cycle-longrun-targets Recursion source of truth: app/src/lib/compute/fiscalAccounting.ts — computeFiscalBlock is the single recursion wired to the displayed debt-to-GDP charts and bands (baseline, scenario, counterfactual, and band paths all go through it). It is a passive accounting recursion: no Bohn primary-balance reaction and no debt-driven risk premium (those live only in the test-only runFiscalRecursion, which has no production caller). There is no separate fiscalProjection.ts file. Law of motion (per quarter, % of GDP): d_t = d_{t-1}·(1+i_q)/(1+g_q) − pb_t/4 + sfa_t/4, with i_q = EFFI/400, g_q = nominal q/q GDP growth (real Δ + deflator Δ), pb = FREV − FPEXP, and the projection using the structural sfaDefault constant (not the noisy forecast SFA column). Snowball = d·(r−g)/(1+g). Debt RISES iff snowball − pb + sfa > 0 (primary deficit, and/or r>g, and/or positive SFA).

All numbers below were reconstructed from the shipped baseline_levels.json + historical_levels.json + fiscal_meta.json for each bloc, replaying the exact computeFiscalBlock recursion — not assumed. Default view ships with consensus anchors OFF (raw model), so the paths below are what users see today.

docs.title: 1. One-line verdict per economy
docs.text: Bloc d0 (2025Q4) Current path (5y / 20q) Root cause Fix US 122.57 FLAT (→121.77, −0.8pp) Snowball −4.4%/yr (g 7.4% ≫ r 3.7%) cancels a too-small −2.5% deficit Cut nominal g to ~3.9%, raise EFFI→5.0, widen deficit to −4.0% → rises to ~143–159 EA 87.85 RISING, too gentle (→93.21, +5.4pp) Favorable snowball −1.4%/yr masks the −2.2% deficit Raise EFFI→2.9, trim g→3.0–3.3 → steeper rise to ~98–100 JP 192.87 FLAT (→196.08, +3.2pp, humped) r≪g snowball −2.4%/yr + late primary surplus anchor Flip pb to −1.5% deficit, raise EFFI→2.0 → rises to ~211 UK 96.24 FALLING (→92.13, −4.1pp) Spurious primary surplus +2.7% (no FREV/FPEXP anchors) Add FREV 39 / FPEXP 41.5 (pb −2.5%), EFFI→4.0 → rises to ~108–112 CA 100.16 FALLING (→90.60, −9.6pp) Spurious surplus +3.1% + oversized SFA +3.19 Add FREV 40.5 / FPEXP 41.5 (pb −1.0%), EFFI→4.0, cut SFA→~0.5 → rises to ~105–108 CN 94.33 RISING, overshoots (→136.52, +42pp) FREV drifts below floor → −8.9% deficit; correct SFA +4.0 Raise FREV target → 25.5 (pb ~−6.5%) → rises to ~120–125 (IMF-augmented-consistent)

docs.title: 2.2 Annual decomposition (% of GDP per year)
docs.text:
Term Value Sign Note Snowball d·(r−g)/(1+g) −4.40 debt-reducing (DOMINANT) r−g = −3.69pp Primary balance pb = FREV−FPEXP −2.49 debt-increasing deficit, but too small vs CBO Structural SFA (sfaDefault) +1.75 debt-increasing held constant Net Δd/yr ≈ −0.16 flat snowball ≈ −(deficit+SFA)

Avg effective rate EFFI = 3.70%/yr; avg nominal growth g = 7.39%/yr; avg pb −2.49%.

docs.title: 2.3 Diagnosis
docs.text:
The engine keeps US debt flat because the snowball is implausibly favorable. Nominal g averages 7.39%/yr (RW/WN-prior-elevated inflation persistence; recent history is 5.4–5.9%) while EFFI only drifts from ~3.2% to ~4.1% (avg 3.70%), locking r−g = −3.69pp. This single term (−4.4%/yr) almost exactly cancels the deficit + SFA. Secondary error: the WN stationary priors revert revenue UP (~17.6% last-hist → ~19% mean) and primary expenditure to ~21.8%, so pb is only −2.5% — CBO is −3 to −4%.

This violates the CBO r→g convergence the most of any bloc: CBO has the effective rate climbing toward nominal g (r−g closing to ~0/slightly positive) as low-coupon debt rolls over; the model locks in r−g = −3.7pp. CBO 2025 Long-Term Budget Outlook has gross debt/GDP RISING ~100%→107% over 5y and to ~120%+ over 10y, with a primary deficit widening toward −4%+.

The current consensus preset in default_anchors.json is also wrong: US.FPEXP_GDP = 17.88 implies a 1.9% primary surplus (US primary spending is ~21–22% of GDP), and FREV_GDP is missing entirely.

docs.title: 2.4 Recommended anchors (terminal-display δc targets at H=20)
docs.text:
Direction is owned by r−g (driftSetter caveat 3), so a CBO-rising path needs BOTH the snowball and the deficit fixed — widening the deficit alone only lifts debt to ~128 because the −4.4%/yr snowball swamps it.

Anchor (US) Set to Units Effect GDPH (real growth) 1.9 % q/q ann nominal g ↓ to ~3.9–4.8% JGDP (deflator) 2.0 % q/q ann (with GDPH) EFFI 5.0 % p.a. r−g closes to ~0/+1pp (CBO convergence) FPEXP_GDP 21.5 % GDP with FREV → pb = −4.0% (CBO-sized) FREV_GDP 17.5 % GDP ADD (currently missing)

Resulting rising path (verified by recursion): with anchors approached over the horizon via the δc forward-pass (partial application, gMult~0.65 on g), debt/GDP rises monotonically 122.6 → ~125 → 128 → 132 → 137 → ~143 (+~20pp/5y). Drivers then read snowball ~−1 to 0%/yr (neutral), primary deficit −4%/yr, SFA +1.75/yr. Held at full steady-state values from t=0 the recursion reaches ~159; the realized path lands between, ~143. Keep SFA at sfaDefault = 1.752.

Milder, debt-held-by-public-style slope: EFFI:4.0, pb −3.0% (FPEXP 21.0 / FREV 18.0), g held ~4.5% → +12–15pp over 5y.

docs.title: 4. How to apply it in the tool
docs.text:
Two mechanisms drive long-run targets, both feeding the δc forward-pass drift setter (driftSetter.ts): - app/public/data/default_anchors.json — the shipped consensus presets per bloc (keyed by variable name, e.g. FREV_GDP, FPEXP_GDP, EFFI, GDPH, JGDP, GDP_<C>, CPI_<C>/HICP_<C>). - The "long-run target" sliders in the UI — the same δc targets, settable interactively (terminal-display value at H=20; lin vars = level, e.g. % of GDP; log vars = % q/q annualized, e.g. growth/inflation/rate).

To put every big-6 debt/GDP on a realistic increasing trajectory, edit default_anchors.json as follows. (SFA changes are in each bloc's fiscal_meta.json sfaDefault, NOT in default_anchors.json.)

"US": { "GDPH": 1.9, "JGDP": 2.0, "UI": 2.3, "LR": 4.2,
        "EFFI": 5.0, "FPEXP_GDP": 21.5, "FREV_GDP": 17.5 },   // FIX FPEXP 17.88→21.5, ADD FREV
"EA": { /* + */ "EFFI": 2.9, "GDP_EA": 1.0 /* trims nominal g */ },
"JP": { "GDP_JP": 0.7, "CPI_JP": 2, "LR_JP": 2.5, "YIELD10_JP": 2,
        "FPEXP_GDP": 35.0, "FREV_GDP": 33.5, "EFFI": 2.0 },    // FLIP 33.3/35 → 35/33.5, ADD EFFI
"UK": { "GDP_UK": 1.3, "CPI_UK": 2, "POLRATE_UK": 2.75, "LR_UK": 4.5, "YIELD10_UK": 3.75,
        "EFFI": 4.0, "FREV_GDP": 39.0, "FPEXP_GDP": 41.5 },    // EFFI 3.5→4.0, ADD FREV+FPEXP
"CA": { "GDP_CA": 1.7, "CPI_CA": 2, "LR_CA": 6,
        "EFFI": 4.0, "FREV_GDP": 40.5, "FPEXP_GDP": 41.5 },    // ADD EFFI+FREV+FPEXP
"CN": { "GDP_CN": 4, "POLRATE_CN": 3, "FPEXP_GDP": 32.0, "FREV_GDP": 25.5 }  // ADD FREV, FPEXP 29.1→32.0
Plus fiscal_meta.json SFA edit: CA sfaDefault: 3.191 → ~0.5. Keep US 1.752, EA 0.325, JP 2.233, UK 3.149 (or trim to ~1.5), CN 4.017.

Why these levers: the debt direction is governed by r−g plus the primary balance. For US/JP the binding fix is raising EFFI toward g (collapsing the free-lunch snowball) and widening/flipping the deficit; for UK/CA it is adding the missing FREV/FPEXP anchors to kill the spurious WN-prior surplus (the single highest-leverage fix); for EA it is steepening an already-rising path; for CN it is moderating an over-steep but correctly-signed path by anchoring revenue.

docs.title: 5. Honesty flag — where rising debt would be UNrealistic
docs.text:
• JP (level). The model's d0 ≈ 193% sits on the GG-gross perimeter, below the ~250% headline. The recommended treatment makes the direction realistic (gently rising, IMF Art-IV-consistent: deficit worsening, interest costs doubling by 2030). But do not read the level as the headline 250% — match direction, not level. Forcing a steeper rise than ~+3.7pp/yr would overstate vs IMF.
  • CN (level/perimeter). d0 = 94.3 and pb = −8.9% sit on the augmented-leaning side of the two IMF perimeters (GG ~88%→110% by 2029 vs augmented ~124%→150%+). The current +42pp overshoots even the augmented GG path; the recommendation moderates it to ~120–125 (between GG and full augmented). A larger rise here would be unrealistic — the SFA already encodes the LGFV channel, so do not also widen the deficit.
  • EA aggregate masks dispersion. The +5.4pp rise is the EA-aggregate; it hides IT/FR (~135/115% rising) vs DE (~63% falling). The 4-var block does not model the SGP/debt-brake consolidation channel — treat the EA rise as an unconstrained aggregate, not a rules-consistent forecast.
  • General caveat. "Realistic rising" means matching the benchmark sign and slope (CBO for US, IMF Fiscal Monitor / WEO for the rest), NOT mechanically forcing every bloc up. EA, JP, CN already rise (CN strongly); only US/UK/CA require flipping a flat/falling artifact, and those flips are anchor-driven corrections of over-optimistic WN-prior means, not fabrications.

docs.title: Fiscal-block expansion — data-availability audit (27 candidate blocs)
docs.text:
Purpose. Extend the 4-variable fiscal block (FREV_GDP, FPEXP_GDP, EFFI, SFA + the debt recursion) to the blocs that lack it. Requested 2026-07-09. Per-economy ingredients audited: quarterly general-government revenue, total expenditure + interest paid (primary expenditure = total − interest), gross debt (d0 seed + SFA residual + back-cast), and the effective interest rate — with the user-sanctioned fallback to the 10-year government bond yield where no interest-paid/maturity data exists. Perimeter (GG vs central government) and seasonal-adjustment seams flagged; the SFA machinery absorbs perimeter seams but they must be declared, never hidden. Sources verified live by the audit agents (Eurostat/BIS APIs fetched; anything unverifiable is marked UNVERIFIED). The no-synthetic-data rule applies throughout: blocked ingredients block the bloc — no interpolation.

Candidates (50 deployed − 23 with fiscal blocks): CH KR MX AU TR SE PL NO DK IN BR RU ID SA AR ZA TH MY CL CO CR CZ HU IL IS NZ TW.

All Eurostat spans below were pulled live from the Eurostat dissemination API (gov_10q_ggnfa, gov_10q_ggdebt, gov_10q_ggfa, vintage 2026-04-22); BIS spans live from the BIS SDMX API (WS_TC); Statistics Iceland from the PX-Web API; FRED/HMB/Minfin via web verification. Anything I could not confirm end-to-end is marked UNVERIFIED. Repo facts read from app/public/data/bvar/<CC>/spec.json and app/public/data/coverage_manifest.json.

Cross-cutting findings

  • SE, PL, DK, CZ, HU, NO are all fully covered by the exact same two Eurostat datasets already used for the 22 existing Eurostat fiscal blocs (FREV_GDP/FPEXP_GDP/EFFI/SFA, source string "national/Eurostat gov-finance"): gov_10q_ggnfa (S13; TR=revenue, TE=total expenditure, D41PAY=interest payable; units MIO_NAC and PC_GDP) + gov_10q_ggdebt (S13, GD, MIO_NAC/PC_GDP). All end 2025Q4 (current). These six slot into the existing pipeline with no new provider.
  • EFFI needs no yield fallback for SE/PL/DK/CZ/HU/NO — D41PAY + lagged GD gives the true effective rate, as in the shipped blocs.
  • Seasonal adjustment: gov_10q_ggnfa is NSA; an SCA (seasonally+calendar adjusted) variant exists for SE/PL/DK/CZ/HU/IS but not for NO or CH (verified empty).
  • The repo's Eurostat 10Y source (irt_lt_mcby_m, Maastricht) does NOT cover NO/IS/CH/TR (verified empty) — a yield fallback for those must come from OECD/FRED or national sources.
  • Coverage-manifest windows read "2015Q4→2025Q4" for everything because the manifest reports the 41-quarter estimation panel, not raw source span; YIELD10 lastObs is 2025Q3 with a nowcast flag to 2025Q4.

docs.title: Recommended build roster (pending user decisions)
docs.text:
• Wave 1 — Eurostat drop-ins (6): SE PL DK CZ HU NO. Same two datasets (gov_10q_ggnfa TR/TE/D41PAY + gov_10q_ggdebt GD) and the same builder as the existing 22 Eurostat fiscal blocs; EFFI direct, no new provider. NO is NSA-only (no SCA variant) — same seasonal handling as other NSA inputs.

Each needs one of: cumulative-monthly differencing (NZ IN CR), a stale-QGFS→national splice (ID MY, TH-style), or a residual verification item (IL CBS quarterly interest detail — the only one left; CO and ZA were verified 2026-07-10 and could equally sit in Wave 2).   • Denominator note: the fiscal builders need quarterly nominal GDP per bloc (fiscal_raw schema: revenue, total_expenditure, interest, gross_debt, nominal_gdp). docs.title: Open decisions (user)
docs.text:
1. CH — no quarterly interest-paid series exists; primary expenditure is therefore not constructible without approximating interest ≈ yield × lagged debt (a modelling choice, not a data splice). Options: (a) skip CH fiscal; (b) 3-variable block without EFFI/interest split; (c) yield-approximated interest, clearly documented. Recommend (a) or (c).
  2. IS — no quarterly GG debt verified anywhere (flows are fine, 2002→2026Q1). Options: skip; or CG-perimeter debt from the central bank (unverified, needs a session with databank.is). Recommend skip for now.
  3. SA — clean but only ~37 quarterly obs (2017Q1→) and no yield to extend backwards. Recommend skip (revisit in 2–3 years) unless a short-sample fiscal block is acceptable.
  4. AR — buildable from 2011 (debt-limited) with the group's worst seams (SPN-vs-AC perimeter, USD debt vs ARS flows, default-era breaks). Recommend: defer to a second pass, or accept 2011→ with heavy documentation.
  5. RU — no fiscal block; consistent with the planned bloc drop.
  6. Perimeter policy — accept central/budgetary-government perimeter for the non-European blocs (IN MY ID TH TW KR NZ CR CO MX CL AR SA TR ZA), labelled per-bloc in the manual's data appendix, with the SFA carrying the seam (as it already does for existing blocs)?
